platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry — What's New advanced to August 2026 (ms.date 2026-09-01), first movement since July
details: **Create a private skill catalog in Foundry Agent Service (public preview).** A skill is "a reusable capability — instructions, bundled scripts, and tool references — that an agent can consume." A private catalog registers organization-scoped skills in **Azure API Center** as assets of type **Skill**, each carrying a title, summary, lifecycle stage, a **Source URL** pointing at the Git repository holding the skill's source, and an **Allowed tools** list naming "the APIs or MCP servers from your API inventory that the skill can access." Microsoft: "The allowed tools list is the governance boundary for a skill." Catalogs can be kept in sync from a Git repo. **Governance → AI Assessment** can score skills against default or custom criteria (name, score range, pass threshold, weight) before promotion. Developer access is gated by the **Azure API Center Data Reader** role; propagation takes up to 24 hours. Discovered in the Foundry portal under **Build > Skills**. `ms.date` 2026-08-19. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/private-skill-catalog

**Long-running agents (preview)** on the `azure-ai-agentserver` packages (`-core` ≥ 2.0.0 GA for Python, `.NET` in preview). New primitives: `@task` and `@multi_turn_task` decorators declaring **crash-resilient units of work**; a `TaskContext` exposing `entry_mode` of `fresh` / `resumed` / **`recovered`**, `retry_attempt`, `RecoveryCount`, `is_steered_turn` and `pending_input_count`; `TaskStatus` of `Pending` / `InProgress` / **`Suspended`** / `Completed`; a `~10 MiB` task payload limit; and `ResponsesServerOptions` flags **`resilient_background`** (re-invoke stored background responses after a crash) and **`steerable_conversations`**, both defaulting to off. A **streaming registry** offers `use_in_memory_live()`, `use_in_memory_replay()` and **`use_file_backed_replay()`** — the last persists stream events to disk and **survives restart**. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/long-running-agent-reference and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/long-running-agent-resilience

**Steer an in-flight agent turn (preview).** With `steerable_conversations=True`, a second turn arriving on a busy conversation **queues and cooperatively cancels the running handler** instead of returning `409 conversation_locked`. The follow-up is sent as a new response with `previous_response_id` set to the running response and the same `agent_session_id`. Ordering is guarded only by an optional `if_last_input_id` precondition ("the input-queue equivalent of an HTTP `If-Match`"); the queue is bounded and raises `SteeringQueueFull`. `ms.date` 2026-08-05. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/steer-hosted-agent

**Bring your own registry for hosted agents.** Foundry hosted agents can be deployed from **container registries outside Azure** — JFrog Artifactory is the validated example; self-hosted Docker Distribution requires a custom authentication adapter. Authentication is **OIDC token exchange**: an Entra application supplies the audience, the **Foundry project managed identity** is the exchanged subject, and the registry issues short-lived pull credentials. The configuration lands as a project connection of category **`CustomKeys`** with `metadata.type=registry_connection` and `mode=oauth_token_exchange`, holding `audience`, `tokenEndpoint` and provider-specific `body.*` keys; the agent definition references it as `registryConnectionId` alongside `docker.imagePassthrough: true`. `ms.date` 2026-09-01 — the newest Foundry page in this scan. Also documented here: the **Foundry RBAC roles were renamed** — Azure AI User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager are now **Foundry User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager**, with role IDs and permissions unchanged. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/private-registry-connections

**Microsoft Foundry Toolkit for Visual Studio Code.** "Foundry Toolkit is the new name for AI Toolkit. It also includes the capabilities previously provided by the separate Microsoft Foundry extension." Ships a **Tool Catalog** to "discover Foundry tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and toolboxes, and then add them to agents"; an **Agent Builder**; an **Agent Inspector** for debugging local agents, streaming responses and tool calls; local model execution through **ONNX, Ollama and Foundry Local**; local GPU fine-tuning; and deployment of hosted agents to Foundry Agent Service **from source code or a container image**. `ms.date` 2026-08-20. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/how-to/develop/get-started-projects-visual-studio-code

*(Also new in the August list, held as extensions of already-reported surfaces: agent optimizer cost/token accounting, a human-in-the-loop approval step, toolbox network isolation, Entra authentication for Foundry Agent trace ingestion, multi-agent orchestration on the Azure OpenAI Responses API, Grok and MAI-Thinking-1 model availability, admin-connected models in cloud evaluations, and a Responsible AI **content provenance** page.)*

findings.title: AWS made organization-wide agent discovery a managed service — every AgentCore Runtime and Gateway in every member account, with no code and no member-account footprint
findings.description: **AWS Agent Registry is now GA**, and its headline launch feature is **auto-detection with AWS Organizations**. A single **organization-scoped registry** (one per Region, owned by the management account or, per AWS's own recommendation, a **delegated administrator**) automatically catalogs **`AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Runtime`** and **`AWS::BedrockAgentCore::Gateway`** resources across every member account, both those that already exist and those created afterward, and stays in sync as resources change and as accounts join or leave the organization. AWS is explicit that the collector is invisible: "there's nothing to install or configure in individual member accounts — **no agents, no per-account permissions, and no member-account resources to set up**." Zenity should treat this as both an ingestion opportunity and a competitive fact — **this is agent inventory as an AWS-native checkbox**, and a customer running it will compare its counts against Zenity's. Four specifics make the comparison winnable, and each is a coverage gap AWS leaves open. **First, the registry cannot tell an MCP server from an agent.** Every runtime protocol — `MCP`, `HTTP`, `A2A`, `AGUI` — maps to `recordType: AGENT`, "because auto-detection can't distinguish a standalone MCP server from an agent that exposes an MCP interface." An operator can hand-narrow a record from `AGENT` to `MCP`, but **the next protocol change silently resets it back to `AGENT` and overrides the narrowing**. Zenity's classification of the same resource should be independent and should be presented as the corrective. **Second, the authorizer detail is deliberately truncated.** Provenance carries the JWT **`discoveryUrl`** and the **`workloadIdentityArn`**, but "other authorizer fields (**`AllowedClients`, `AllowedAudience`, `AllowedScopes`**) are not carried into the record" — precisely the fields that answer *who may call this agent*. A registry-derived inventory therefore cannot evaluate authorization scope; Zenity's must read the source resource. **Third, deprecation silently freezes truth.** "If you deprecate an auto-detected record… auto-detection stops syncing changes from the source resource to that record. Subsequent updates — such as protocol, authorizer, or endpoint changes — are not applied." A deprecated record is a stale record that still looks like a record, and it is a plausible evasion: change a runtime's authorizer after its registry entry is deprecated and the catalog never notices. **Fourth, auto-detected records cannot be deleted while auto-detection is on**, and refreshes to an already-approved record are written as a new `Draft` revision that is undiscoverable until approved — so the discoverable view of an agent can lag its actual configuration indefinitely if no curator approves. AISPM should ingest organization-scoped registries via `agent-registry-control`, key on the `aws-autodetected-` name prefix and the `DETECTED_FROM` provenance relation to separate detected from hand-authored records, resolve each `sourceId` ARN back to the owning member account, reconcile the registry's agent list against Zenity's own AgentCore discovery in both directions, and flag deprecated auto-detected records, unapproved draft revisions, and `autoDetectionConfiguration.enabled=true` with `autoDetection.status=INACTIVE` — a state AWS documents as reachable and which means the org believes discovery is running when it is not

findings.title: AgentCore Memory's new `IngestData` API writes into long-term memory with no event, no conversation and no retrievable record of what was written
findings.description: `IngestData` submits content "directly for long-term memory extraction, **without persisting it as a short-term memory event**." The consequence is stated plainly in the same paragraph: "the submitted content **cannot be retrieved with `GetEvent`, `ListEvents`, or `ListSessions`**, or reorganized with branching." This closes a progression this monitor has been tracking. On **2026-08-23** AgentCore Memory accepted a `json` payload type on `CreateEvent`, and the finding then was that **the memory write path no longer requires a conversation**. `IngestData` removes the remaining constraint: the write path no longer requires an **event** either. What lands in long-term memory — the store that shapes every future session for that `actorId` — now has no durable record of its own arrival on any of the three enumeration APIs an investigator would reach for. AWS frames this as a storage-cost optimization ("avoid the short-term storage overhead of persisting an event you would never read back"), and the framing is honest, but the security property is that **memory poisoning through this path is not merely undetected, it is unenumerable after the fact**. Both payload types are accepted — `conversational` messages with a `USER`/`ASSISTANT` role, and arbitrary `json` "such as behavioral events, activity logs, or system events" — and both **fan out to every configured long-term strategy except self-managed ones**, meaning semantic, user-preference, summarization and episodic extraction all consume it. Content sharing an `actorId`, `sessionId` and namespace "is treated as related context during extraction," so an attacker who can call `IngestData` for a victim's `actorId` can influence how that user's genuine interactions are summarized. AIDR should treat **`IngestData` as a first-class activity type distinct from `CreateEvent`** and alert on it specifically — an IAM principal that calls `IngestData` but never `CreateEvent` is writing memory without writing history. Because the data plane offers no retrospective view, the only durable signals are external: **CloudTrail on the `IngestData` call**, the **Kinesis memory-record stream** AWS documents for real-time notification when memory records are created, and `ListMemoryExtractionJobs` for the failure queue. AISPM should inventory which memory resources have long-term strategies configured (that is what makes them `IngestData` targets), enumerate every principal holding the `IngestData` permission as a distinct privilege class from event creation, and treat the ability to write another actor's namespace as a toxic combination. The companion **flexible namespaces** release in the same batch widens the blast radius by making namespaces variable rather than fixed. Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/long-term-ingest-data.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/APIReference/API_IngestData.html

findings.title: Foundry's private skill catalog makes a skill an inventory entity with a declared tool-reach boundary — and that boundary is enforced from an Azure API Center Zenity does not currently read
findings.description: Foundry Agent Service now supports a **private skill catalog** (public preview) in which a skill — "instructions, bundled scripts, and tool references" — is registered as an **asset in Azure API Center** with a title, summary, lifecycle stage, a **Source URL** naming the Git repository that holds its code, and, critically, an **Allowed tools** list specifying "the APIs or MCP servers from your API inventory that the skill can access." Microsoft's own language sets the stakes: "**The allowed tools list is the governance boundary for a skill.** It explicitly defines which resources the skill can consume, so a shared skill can't reach endpoints you didn't approve." That sentence is the finding. A skill is now a **first-class, permissioned, organization-shared unit of agent capability** whose authorization is declared in a *different Azure service* from the agent that consumes it — so an agent's effective reach is the union of its own tool connections and the allowed-tools lists of every catalog skill it loads, and neither view alone is complete. Four properties compound this. **Skills are Git-backed and can auto-sync**: "integrate a Git repository with your API Center" keeps the catalog in sync with source, which means **a commit to a repository changes what a shared, organization-wide agent capability does, with no Azure control-plane event**. **Access is a single coarse RBAC grant** — Azure API Center Data Reader over the API Center resource — so catalog membership is all-or-nothing per reader, not per skill. **Quality gating is model-scored, not policy-enforced**: API Center's **AI Assessment** scores skills against "default or custom criteria (name, score range, pass threshold, and weight)" before promotion, which is an LLM-adjacent judgement standing in for a review gate. And **role assignments take up to 24 hours to propagate**, so revoking a developer's catalog access is not immediate. AISPM should discover **Azure API Center resources linked to Foundry projects**, inventory registered **Skill** assets as a new entity type carrying their `Source URL` repository and their allowed-tools list, resolve each allowed tool to the actual API or **MCP server** it names, compute per-agent effective reach as the union across loaded skills, and build toxic-combination rules for: a skill whose allowed tools include a write-capable MCP server; a skill sourced from a repository outside the organization's control or with broad write access; a catalog with AI Assessment disabled; and a skill whose Git sync means its content today differs from the content assessed at promotion. This is architecturally the same problem as the AgentCore skill catalog reported 2026-08-21, but with the governance boundary externalized into a separate Azure resource — Zenity's Foundry collector must now read Azure API Center or it will systematically understate what Foundry agents can reach

findings.title: Foundry hosted agents can now be redirected mid-execution by a second caller, and their durable task state survives the process that created it
findings.description: The **long-running agents** preview introduces two properties that break assumptions AIRT and AIDR currently rely on. **First, steering.** With `steerable_conversations=True` on `ResponsesServerOptions`, or `steerable=True` on a `@multi_turn_task`, a second input arriving on a conversation that is **already executing a turn** no longer gets `409 conversation_locked` and no longer races — it **queues behind the active turn and the framework signals the running handler to cooperatively wind down**, after which the queued input takes over and reports `ctx.is_steered_turn == True`. The only ordering guard is an **optional** `if_last_input_id` precondition that the caller must remember to pass ("the input-queue equivalent of an HTTP `If-Match`"); omit it and any caller who can post to the conversation can interrupt and redirect work already in flight. Microsoft's own example is a user changing "Plan a trip to Rome" to "Actually, Paris" mid-execution — the benign framing of an operation that, in an agent with tool access, means **abandoning a partially-executed plan at an arbitrary boundary and starting a new one with the partial side effects already committed**. AIRT should probe exactly that: whether a steered handoff can leave an agent having performed the first half of one instruction and the second half of another, whether `partial_result` returned at a cancellation boundary is fed into the next turn's context, and whether a steering input can arrive from a principal other than the one that started the turn. **Second, durability.** Tasks are **crash-resilient**: a handler that dies is **re-invoked with the persisted input** and `entry_mode: "recovered"`, and crash recovery "re-enters the same attempt and doesn't consume retry budget" — so a handler can be re-entered an unbounded number of times without tripping the retry policy. `resilient_background=True` re-invokes stored background responses after a restart. Task inputs are persisted before the handler runs, up to a `~10 MiB` payload, and **`use_file_backed_replay()` persists the event stream to disk so it survives restart**. Together these create durable agent state — task inputs, checkpointed response snapshots (`context.persisted_response`), cross-turn `conversation_chain_metadata` watermarks, and on-disk stream replay buffers — that **outlives the container and is invisible to any point-in-time inventory of running agents**. AISPM should treat resilient task records, steering queues and file-backed stream directories as agent-adjacent data stores holding conversation content, and should flag `steerable_conversations` and `resilient_background` as posture attributes (both default to `False`; turning them on changes the concurrency and persistence model). AIDR should model `entry_mode: recovered` and `is_steered_turn` as activity qualifiers — a turn that executes twice under recovery, or that runs under a different instruction than the one that started it, will otherwise look like duplicate or inconsistent activity rather than the documented behavior it is. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/steer-hosted-agent and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/long-running-agent-reference

findings.title: Anthropic shipped a second safeguards-lifted model, and this one documents a security check it deliberately skips
findings.description: **Claude Mythos 5.1 (`claude-mythos-5-1`)** GA'd on **September 1** as the successor to Mythos 5 — the model established on 2026-08-23 to be **Claude Fable 5 with its real-time safety classifiers removed** — and **AWS published a Bedrock model card for it the same day**. Access is unchanged and remains the operative risk: entitlement runs through **Anthropic, AWS or Google Cloud account teams** under **Project Glasswing**, so a Zenity customer can be running it on infrastructure Zenity already monitors without any procurement signal Zenity would see, and the reason the 2026-08-23 finding still holds is that **guardrail behaviour is a property of the deployment, not the model** — a refusal-based probe against Mythos passes exactly as it would against Fable, because the *model* is the same weights. Two things are new and both are actionable. **First, Anthropic now documents a security-relevant behavioural divergence between the two.** Fable 5.1 enforces a **thinking-block prefix-integrity check**: modifying the `system` prompt, the `tools` array, or any earlier message invalidates every later thinking block, and a replayed block is rejected with a 400 reading `The block is bound to a different conversation`. This is a genuine tamper-detection primitive — it makes silent rewriting of an agent's conversation history a hard error. Anthropic then states, in one sentence: "**Claude Mythos 5.1 doesn't run this check.**" So the safeguards-lifted variant is also the variant on which conversation history can be edited between turns without the API objecting. **That is a distinguishing signal Zenity can actually test for**, and it is far more reliable than probing refusals: construct a two-turn conversation, alter the earlier turn, replay the thinking block, and observe whether the deployment returns 400 or proceeds. AIRT should build that as a deployment-fingerprinting probe and use it to detect Mythos entitlement on Bedrock, Vertex and direct-API paths where the model ID may be aliased. **Second, `tool_choice` forcing is gone on both models** — `{"type": "any"}` and `{"type": "tool", "name": "..."}` now return a **400** — which means any Zenity control, harness or red-team fixture that pins a model to a specific tool call will break silently against these models and fall back to `auto`, changing what the model actually does under test. AISPM should add `claude-mythos-5-1` to the model-inventory watchlist across all three clouds, and treat the presence of any Mythos identifier in a customer's Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry model access configuration as a HIGH posture finding on its own — the model is entitled per-account, so its presence is evidence of a deliberate, negotiated exception to standard safety configuration. Note also that both new models carry **1M-token context as the default and maximum**, so a single request can now carry an entire corpus, and Anthropic's own migration guidance describes Fable 5.1 as **more likely to rewrite whole files than make targeted edits** — a materially larger blast radius per agent action. Sources: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/fable-5-1/whats-new-fable-5-1 and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-card-anthropic-claude-mythos-5-1.html

findings.title: Kiro now pushes cloud-stored agent configuration — including MCP-bundling "Powers" — down into local IDE and CLI sessions
findings.description: Kiro's **Configuration Sync** went GA on **September 1**: it "bridges cloud settings to local IDE and CLI sessions," syncing **Steering files, custom agents, Skills, Powers and Hooks** without replacing local files. Read alongside what this monitor already recorded about Kiro on 2026-08-23 — that custom agent config files carry an **`mcpServers` field naming which MCP servers that agent may reach**, that MCP config exists at both workspace and user scope, and that a **file watcher on `.kiro/agents` and `mcp.json` hot-reloads changes mid-session with no restart and no UI event** — this closes a loop that should concern ENDPOINT directly. **A remote, cloud-side configuration change can now alter a local agent's tool grants and MCP server list, on a developer's machine, mid-session, without a restart, without a user action, and without a local control-plane event to observe.** Kiro's documentation makes the reach explicit: "your steering files, permissions, hooks, MCP servers, and custom agents work identically whether you're in the IDE, CLI, or Web, with your `.kiro/` configuration shared across all of them." The **Powers** primitive is the sharpest element — Powers "bundle MCP tools with knowledge and workflows" and "**activate dynamically based on context**," so the set of MCP tools live in a session is a runtime function of context rather than a static declaration, and is exactly the object now being synced from the cloud. Zenity's own prior finding that **Kiro hides plugin-format MCP servers from `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`** compounds this: the file an endpoint agent would read is already an incomplete view, and now a second, remote source of truth writes into the same effective configuration. ENDPOINT should enumerate the `.kiro/` tree at both workspace and user scope **plus** Powers and plugin-format servers that do not appear in `mcp.json`, capture configuration state as a time series rather than a snapshot because it changes without process restart, and treat a Configuration Sync event as a capability-change event requiring re-inventory. Two further items from the same release matter for scoping: **Kiro Web is now GA**, adding a browser surface where work is delegated to agents entirely outside the endpoint's visibility, and **OpenTelemetry metrics export** now sends per-user Kiro usage over OTLP to CloudWatch, Datadog, Dynatrace, Elastic, Honeycomb and OpenSearch, which is a telemetry stream Zenity could ingest where a customer already collects it. Kiro remains **absent from `sources.json`** for the fourth consecutive scan despite being AWS's named successor to the Amazon Q Developer IDE plugins retiring 2027-04-30. Sources: https://kiro.dev/changelog/ and https://kiro.dev/docs/cloud-sessions/

findings.title: Codex extensions can now replace an MCP tool result before the model sees it
findings.description: **Codex CLI 0.151.0** (August 29) added "extension-level MCP tool result **inspection/replacement**." This is a supported, in-process interception point sitting between an MCP server and the language model, and it cuts both ways for Zenity. **Defensively it is an integration path** — an extension in this position can inspect tool output for injected instructions, redact secrets before they enter context, or enforce policy on what a tool is allowed to return, which is a stronger placement than anything available through Codex's existing hook surface. **Offensively it is a new supply-chain component with model-facing write access**: an extension that can *replace* a tool result can fabricate one, and the model has no way to distinguish a replaced result from a genuine one. Codex's plugin distribution is the delivery mechanism, and the same release changed it — "plugin catalogs now combine per-repository configuration while reporting invalid marketplaces separately" — meaning **a repository can contribute plugin sources to a developer's Codex session**, which is the [[agent-plugins-cross-vendor-standard]] pattern arriving in another client. Two adjacent items from the same version run compound the surface. **Codex CLI 0.150.0** added **`@` task mentions "enabling agents to read/create/message tasks"** — agents writing into and messaging through the task system, i.e. agent-to-agent and agent-to-human communication through a channel Zenity does not currently model — plus new **`Interrupt` hooks** covering interrupted-turn commands and MCP handlers. **Codex CLI 0.152.0/0.152.1** added **per-tool MCP `output_token_limit`** (a per-tool truncation setting, which is also a per-tool evidence-loss setting for anything inspecting tool output), app-server `thread/shellCommand` timeouts **exceeding one hour**, and the note that "Guardian approval review now honors **Node REPL policies provided through model metadata**" — a policy input arriving with the model rather than from local configuration. AIDR should model extension-mediated MCP result replacement as an activity type and treat divergence between a server's emitted result and the model's received result as a detection signal; ENDPOINT should inventory installed Codex extensions and per-repository plugin catalog sources as a distinct class from MCP servers, since an extension is strictly more privileged than the servers it mediates. Sources: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog and https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp

findings.title: Foundry hosted agents can now run container images pulled from registries outside Azure
findings.description: **Bring your own registry** (page dated 2026-09-01, the newest Foundry article this scan) lets a Foundry hosted agent be deployed from "a container image stored in an authenticated container registry **outside Azure**, such as **JFrog Artifactory** or a self-hosted **Docker Distribution** registry." Authentication is **OIDC token exchange**: an Entra application supplies the audience, the **Foundry project managed identity** is the exchanged subject, and the external registry issues short-lived pull credentials, so **no registry secret is stored** — good hygiene that also removes the credential artifact an inventory might otherwise notice. The configuration materializes as a Foundry project connection of category **`CustomKeys`** carrying `metadata.type=registry_connection` and `mode=oauth_token_exchange` with `audience`, `tokenEndpoint` and arbitrary provider-specific `body.<field>` keys, and the agent definition references it as **`registryConnectionId`** alongside **`docker.imagePassthrough: true`**. The security consequence is a supply-chain one: **the image an agent runs is no longer required to exist in any Azure resource**, so an inventory that enumerates Azure Container Registries to answer "what code is this agent running" now has a blind spot, and provenance for the running agent terminates at a hostname outside the tenant's Azure footprint. Microsoft also notes that the **Docker Distribution path requires a customer-built authentication adapter** for which "Foundry doesn't define a universal request and response contract" — a bespoke, customer-implemented component standing in the agent's image-pull path. AISPM should enumerate Foundry project connections with `metadata.type=registry_connection` as a distinct entity, resolve each agent's `registryConnectionId` and record the external registry host as the agent's image provenance, flag `docker.imagePassthrough: true` agents whose image origin is outside the tenant, and treat the Entra application created for the audience value as an agent-supply-chain principal. **Operational note from the same page**: the Foundry RBAC roles were renamed — **Azure AI User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager are now Foundry User / Owner / Account Owner / Project Manager**, with role IDs and permissions unchanged. Any Zenity rule, query or report that matches Foundry roles by display name will silently stop matching

findings.title: Anthropic added personal and service-account API keys that can reach admin endpoints across every workspace
findings.description: On **August 27** Anthropic introduced **personal keys** and **service account keys** in the Claude Console. They "act as you or as a service account, with the same permissions, and stop working when the linked account is removed from an organization" — and, critically, "these API keys can be **scoped to a specific workspace** or **work on admin endpoints and across any workspace the account has access to**." That second mode is the finding: a single credential can now carry a human's or a service account's full organizational reach, including admin-endpoint access, rather than being bounded to one workspace as the legacy workspace API keys were. Anthropic's stated benefit — that admins "can more easily track usage for each account, and ensure key usage is legitimate" — is real, and the lifecycle binding (the key dies when the account leaves the org) closes an orphaned-credential gap. But the same change means **the blast radius of one leaked key is now the account's entire permission set** rather than one workspace, and a personal key acting *as a named human* makes credential-versus-human attribution harder in exactly the logs used for investigation. This lands alongside the workload identity federation and service account surface documented in the Admin API's move into the SDKs on August 26. AISPM should inventory Claude organization credentials by **type** — personal key, service account key, legacy workspace key — via the Admin API's API-keys endpoints, treat any key whose scope is organization-wide rather than workspace-bound as a privileged credential, map personal keys to their owning human and service account keys to their service account, and flag the combination of an organization-scoped personal key held by a user with admin rights. AIDR should attribute API activity through the key type, since a personal key's actions are indistinguishable from the human's own unless the key identity is resolved

findings.title: Anthropic's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards moves transcript storage and misuse detection into the customer's own cloud bucket
findings.description: **Enterprise Frontier Safeguards**, announced **September 1** and developed with over 100 enterprises including Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citi, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Mastercard, Visa, Stripe, Salesforce, Snowflake, Comcast and KPMG, resolves the zero-data-retention-versus-misuse-detection tension by **storing customer data in infrastructure the enterprise controls — AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage — under the customer's own encryption keys and access policies**, with **automated detection only** and flags routed **directly to the customer** rather than to Anthropic human reviewers. Detection is **pattern-based across multiple sessions and accounts over rolling time windows**. It spans **Claude Code, Claude Enterprise, the Claude Platform, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry**, with phased rollout beginning **fall 2026**. Three consequences for Zenity, all inventory-shaped. **First, a new storage entity**: an EFS-enabled organization has a customer-owned bucket holding Claude session content — including, by extension of the Compliance API surface documented on 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-26, **local Claude Code and Cowork transcripts and `office_agents` sessions**. That bucket is a high-value data store that AISPM should discover, and whose access policy, encryption key and public-exposure posture should be assessed like any other sensitive corpus. **Second, a new detection stream the customer owns**: misuse flags land with the enterprise, which makes them ingestible — AIDR should treat EFS detections as a first-party signal source rather than a vendor-internal one, and should reconcile them against Zenity's own findings on the same sessions. **Third, and most important, EFS changes the meaning of "ZDR" in a Claude deployment.** The Compliance API's documented blind spots already state that **ZDR sessions are excluded** from transcript retrieval — so an organization that adopts EFS specifically to obtain ZDR is, by that route, opting out of the Compliance API path Zenity may currently rely on, while gaining a bucket Zenity must instead read. AISPM should detect which retention mode a customer's Claude organization is in and route collection accordingly, and should flag the transition itself, because an org moving to EFS will look like a collection outage if the bucket is not onboarded at the same time. Note that Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 "aren't available under zero data retention unless expressly authorized by Anthropic," so EFS and the newest models interact in ways worth confirming per tenant

findings.title: The Microsoft Foundry Toolkit for VS Code merges two extensions into one local surface that discovers MCP servers and deploys hosted agents
findings.description: **Foundry Toolkit** "is the new name for AI Toolkit. It also includes the capabilities previously provided by the separate Microsoft Foundry extension" — so a single VS Code extension now spans local model execution and cloud agent deployment, and two extension identifiers a discovery tool might have tracked separately collapse into one. Its capabilities read as an endpoint inventory checklist: a **Tool Catalog** that discovers "Foundry tools, **Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers**, and toolboxes" and adds them to agents; an **Agent Builder** that configures instructions, models, variables, structured outputs and tools **without creating an agent code project** — so an agent can exist with no file in source control; an **Agent Inspector** that debugs local agents and inspects streaming responses and tool calls; local model execution through **ONNX, Ollama and Foundry Local**; local GPU fine-tuning; and deployment of hosted agents to Foundry Agent Service **from source code or a container image**, plus browsing and versioning of cloud agents from inside the editor. The composite risk is the same shape as the Cursor and Kiro findings of the last two scans: **a developer workstation is now a place where an agent can be authored, given MCP tool grants, tested against local models, and pushed to a production Foundry project without leaving the IDE**, and the MCP servers it discovers are configured through the extension rather than through the Azure control plane. ENDPOINT should add the Foundry Toolkit extension to its discovery target set (noting the rename from AI Toolkit, which will break identifier-based detection), enumerate the MCP servers and toolboxes it registers locally, and treat a workstation holding both the Toolkit and a signed-in Foundry project as a deployment path into that project. AISPM should correlate hosted agents in a Foundry project back to the workstation and identity that deployed them, since `azd`-based and Toolkit-based deployment leave different traces than portal-created agents

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise brought federated data stores into FedRAMP High Assured Workloads and extended DLP content policies to connectors, apps and notebooks
findings.description: Two GA items dated **August 31**. **Federated data stores in Assured Workloads** lets Google Workspace and third-party **federated** connectors be attached to projects inside **Assured Workloads folders**, which enforce **FedRAMP High** controls — and Google confirms that third-party federated connectors at GA or Public Preview are in scope for its FedRAMP High authorization, as is the Google federated connector covering **Gmail, Drive and Calendar**. The mechanism is what matters: a **federated** data store is not indexed into Gemini Enterprise — "Gemini Enterprise sends your search query **directly to the third-party API**" and blends the results — so an agent operating inside a FedRAMP High boundary now issues live queries out to third-party SaaS APIs at request time. **The compliance boundary and the data-flow boundary are not the same boundary**, and an inventory that enumerates data stores without distinguishing federated from indexed will materially misstate where a regulated workload's queries actually go. AISPM should record **federation mode** as an attribute of every Gemini Enterprise data store, and should flag federated connectors attached to Assured Workloads projects as a distinct posture case requiring per-connector egress review. The companion item, **Sensitive Data Protection content policies** applied to **connectors, apps and notebooks**, is the constructive half — a first-party DLP control now exists at three levels of the Gemini Enterprise object model, which means **its absence is now a detectable posture gap**: AISPM should assess, per connector, per app and per notebook, whether an SDP content policy is attached, and treat an unpoliced connector in an organization that uses the feature elsewhere as an inconsistency finding. Both items continue the read-to-write and reach-expansion pattern reported on 2026-08-21 and 2026-08-30, where Google widens what already-connected data stores can do without the connector list changing. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/release-notes and https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores

findings.title: ServiceNow can publish its own agents into Microsoft Agent 365 — a cross-platform agent path with zero prior coverage
findings.description: The AI Control Tower release notes list, under **Australia Patch 2**, the "**Ability to publish ServiceNow agents to Microsoft Agent 365**." That capability returns **zero hits across every report this monitor has written**, and it completes a picture the 2026-08-30 scan opened from the Microsoft side. Agent 365 was found then to **auto-ingest AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI agents "via the Google and Amazon APIs" with no SDK integration and no code change** — a pull model. This is the complementary **push** model: a ServiceNow administrator can publish ServiceNow-built agents into a Microsoft tenant's Agent 365 registry, so a customer's Microsoft agent inventory can contain agents that were authored, and are still governed, in ServiceNow. The governance consequence is that **the agent has two control planes and they do not agree**: ServiceNow's AI Control Tower can deactivate or reinstate it, Entra can mint or disable its agent identity, and Defender's real-time protection covers it only through the Work IQ MCP path documented on 2026-08-30. AISPM should not treat an Agent 365 record and a ServiceNow AI Control Tower record for the same agent as two agents; it should establish the ServiceNow→Agent 365 publication relationship as an inventory edge, determine which platform is authoritative for the agent's tool and connector grants, and flag published agents whose ServiceNow-side permissions exceed what the Agent 365 view shows. Note the source caveat that produced this: the family index at `servicenow.com/docs/r/release-notes/family-release-notes.html` — the URL in `sources.json` — asserts no feature content at all, and this item is only visible on the per-application `ai-control-tower-rn.html` page, which is itself stale (`Last Updated: March 12, 2026`)

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic) — Model Hardware Standard, announced 2026-08-27
details: **The Model Hardware Standard (MHS)**, a research preview opened to a first group of scientific research labs and advanced manufacturers, co-developed with **HHMI Janelia Research Campus**. A standardized software driver translates between operating systems and hardware devices using two primitives, **`read`** (retrieve data such as temperature) and **`write`** (set parameters). Devices become **discoverable in a standardized format**, so agents and instruments locate each other across networks with no custom translator programs. Drivers carry **natural-language metadata tags** documenting weight, capabilities and **safety limits** — information previously only in manuals or tacit knowledge — and auto-generate the reference files agents need. Orchestration runs over three interfaces: **Model Context Protocol (MCP), command-line interfaces, and code file APIs**. Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-hardware-standard-research-preview

**Demonstrated device classes**: liquid handlers, 6-DoF robotic arms, microplate readers, two-photon and light-sheet microscopy, thermocyclers, qPCR instruments, centrifuges, incubators, cameras, sensors, laser systems and optical components. Source: same

**Safety controls as documented**: device-level safety limits enforced by MHS drivers (laser power, mechanical ranges); agents "often stopped to wait for human confirmation before performing an action it deemed even slightly risky"; Carnegie Mellon induced six failure scenarios — missing plate, rotated plate, reader busy, disconnected camera, unreachable device, emergency stop — and the system "correctly blocked all six before any device moved." Source: same

**Ecosystem**: preview participants Genentech, University of Washington (Baker and Pinglay labs), Carnegie Mellon, HHMI Janelia, QuEra Computing, Tetsuwan Scientific. Platform partners building **native MHS support**: **AWS/Strands, Tecan, QIAGEN, Universal Robots**. Model-agnostic; Anthropic intends to open-source the standard. Applications at `modelhardwarestandard.com` — which is an application gate only, with the technical specification restricted to approved participants. Source: https://modelhardwarestandard.com

*(Held: the platform release notes moved to **August 27**, but only to record that `client.beta.files` and `client.beta.skills` stop sending the `files-api-2025-04-14` and `skills-2025-10-02` beta headers and now match the non-beta shapes, with `BetaSkill` renamed `BetaContainerSkill`. An SDK shape migration, not a new capability.)*

*(Held: "Expanding our support for scientists," also August 27 — 10,000 free/discounted Claude seats for scientists, the AI for Science program broadened beyond biology, up to $50,000 credits per project. Access expansion of the already-reported Claude Science, with no new API, connector or agent surface.)*

platforms.name: Microsoft Defender / Agent 365 — first read of an entire agent-security product line
details: **Local AI agent discovery (Defender for Endpoint, Preview).** Defender automatically discovers supported local AI agents **and MCP server configurations — local and remote** — on onboarded **Windows and macOS** devices. Defender defines an agent as the tuple **(user, device, agent type)**, so Claude Code running in 15 project folders for one user on one device is a single inventory entry. Three surfaces: **local AI agent inventory** (device and user associations, discovery metadata), an **exposure map** of relationships between agents, devices, identities and the resources those identities can reach, and **advanced hunting in KQL**. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/local-agent-discovery-overview

**The enumerated supported-agent taxonomy** — *CLI*: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Junie CLI, Kiro CLI, OpenCode, Warp, Antigravity CLI. *Desktop*: ChatGPT Desktop, Claude Desktop, Codex Desktop, Goose Desktop, Hermes Agent, Ollama Desktop, Perplexity Desktop, Poe Desktop. *Agentic IDEs*: Cursor, Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf), Kiro IDE, Antigravity IDE. *VS Code extensions*: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Gemini Code Assist, GitHub Copilot, Roo Code. *Claw-based*: **OpenClaw, Clawpilot, QClaw, Claw/Nanobot**. Source: same

**AI agent runtime protection (Defender for Endpoint, Preview).** Device-level prompt-injection detection and blocking, inspecting three points in the agent loop: the **user prompt**, the **pre-tool call** before execution, and the **post-tool response**. Two methods, each with `Disabled` / `Audit` / `Block` modes set via `Set-MpPreference`: **`AiAgentProtection`** (agent-native event inspection over vendor hook interfaces — Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app) and **`AiAgentNetworkInspection`** (inspects agent-to-LLM network flows for agents with no hook interface). Alert name is **"Suspicious AI prompt injection."** Requires Defender for Endpoint P2 / M365 E5 / Agent 365 / M365 E7, AV in active mode, signature `1.451.224.0`+. **No native Intune policy support** — deployment is a PowerShell platform script run in system context. Setting is under tamper protection. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/ai-agent-runtime-protection-overview and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection

**Security for AI (Defender XDR)** turns on automatically when a tenant onboards to Agent 365 — the Enable toggle is **on by default**. Cloud/platform agent discovery spans **Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry, AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI**, plus M365 Copilot Agent Builder and any agent built with the Agent 365 SDK. Named detection scenarios: **indirect prompt injection, evasion techniques, malicious content propagation, secret leakage, LLM reconnaissance, suspicious IP access**. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/security-for-ai/defender-security-for-ai

**Real-time protection rules.** A built-in **Default rule audits all agents**; **custom rules block** and are scoped to all or specific agents with an exclude list. Selectable detection types: **Secret exfiltration, Malicious content propagation, Evasion techniques, Unsafe email domain**. Audited and blocked activity is written as behaviours to the **`BehaviorInfo`** table. Coverage differs sharply by agent type: Agent 365 agents are covered **only through Work IQ MCP** ("agents that rely on unsupported tools or don't integrate with Work IQ MCP aren't covered"); Copilot Studio agents are evaluated at tool invocation; **Foundry agents are evaluated on user requests, agent responses, tool invocations *and* tool responses**. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/security-for-ai/ai-agent-real-time-protection

**Copilot Studio external threat detection provider (Preview).** A documented two-endpoint REST contract — `POST /validate` and `POST /analyze-tool-execution` at `api-version=2025-05-01` — called every time the orchestrator considers invoking a tool, returning `{"blockAction": true|false}`. Only invoked on **generative agents using generative orchestration**; **skipped for classic agents**. Entra auth via **Federated Identity Credentials**, set up with `Create-CopilotWebhookApp.ps1`. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/external-security-provider and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/external-security-webhooks-interface-developers

platforms.name: Google Gemini Enterprise — release notes advanced to 2026-08-28
details: **Five new data stores in public preview**: **Campfire, Clay, CourtListener, Daloopa, MSCI** — "search and read data from these data stores using natural language." Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/msci

**Three existing data stores gained write actions**: **AirOps** — "Update knowledge base document metadata"; **Airtable** — "Create records for a table"; **Zoho Desk** — "Update event." Source: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/manage-actions

*(Note: `cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/release-notes` in `sources.json` 301-redirects to `docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/release-notes`, which tops at August 23 with an Agent Platform Workbench dependency refresh — no agent-surface delta on that stream.)*

platforms.name: Cursor (watching tier) — changelog advanced to 2026-08-27
details: **"Start from scratch" — Cloud Agents no longer need any source-control connection.** Selecting *Start from scratch* in the repo picker and prompting the agent causes Cursor to **create an Origin repository in the background**; the user later clicks *Create repo* to name it and set visibility (private or internal), and the scaffolded repository appears in the Codebase tab. Source: https://cursor.com/changelog/start-from-scratch
**In-browser live preview.** Cursor "port-forwards your cloud agent's live environment straight to your browser," giving real-time preview and design-mode access during the session. Source: same

**Publish with Vercel.** Connecting a Vercel account deploys the agent's work to a **live URL**. Sources: same and https://vercel.com/changelog/deploy-cursor-origin-repositories-with-vercel-in-public-beta

platforms.name: Salesforce AgentForce — coverage-gap recovery (GA since 2026-04-29)
details: **Agentforce Operations** — the productized form of the **Regrello acquisition, which closed October 1, 2025** — extends Agentforce agents from front-office experiences **into back-office processes and systems: email, ERP and collaboration tools**, for "end-to-end agentic execution across the back office," on the explicit premise that "agents are designed to complete work rather than route it." **Specialized back-office agents** "autonomously perform work across disconnected systems from email to ERP," and "extract data from complex documents, run computations, update credit models and identify compliance gaps," handling data verification, approvals and compliance checks. Ships **30+ out-of-the-box blueprint templates** (invoice auditing, onboarding, PO rescheduling) and can **generate blueprints from unstructured process documents**. Work surfaces into **Slack and Microsoft Teams**; processes are edited with plain-language updates by business users **without code**; **auto-sync and Salesforce Flow triggering** were slated for beta in May 2026. Claimed effect: cycle times cut up to 70%, 80% of manual tasks eliminated, "audit-ready outcomes at scale." Source: https://www.salesforce.com/agentforce/operations/
*(Winter '27, published 2026-08-19, remains unverifiable from any Salesforce-hosted source — sixth consecutive scan. Dreamforce runs 2026-09-12 to 09-14 and is the larger expected delta.)*

findings.title: Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard puts agent tool calls on the other side of a robot arm, a laser and a centrifuge
findings.description: On **August 27, 2026** Anthropic opened a research preview of the **Model Hardware Standard**, "a shared specification for AI agents to safely operate physical devices," co-developed with HHMI Janelia and being adopted natively by **AWS/Strands, Tecan, QIAGEN and Universal Robots**. The architecture matters more than the announcement. A **standardized driver** exposes exactly two primitives — **`read`** and **`write`** — to any device with a programmable interface. **Device discovery is standardized**, so "agents and instruments locate each other across networks" with no custom translator program, meaning the set of devices an agent can reach is a *network* property, not a configuration file. Drivers embed **natural-language metadata including the device's safety limits**, which is simultaneously the safety control and a machine-readable description of exactly what the limits are. Orchestration runs over **MCP, CLIs and code file APIs** — so the same MCP transport AIRT already models for data exfiltration now carries actuation. The demonstrated device set is liquid handlers, **6-DoF robotic arms**, microplate readers, two-photon and light-sheet microscopes, thermocyclers, qPCR instruments, centrifuges, incubators, cameras, sensors and **laser systems**. The documented controls are thin and explicitly probabilistic: driver-enforced device limits, plus an agent that "**often** stopped to wait for human confirmation before performing an action it deemed even slightly risky" — a model-judgement gate, not a policy gate. Carnegie Mellon's validation covers *hardware-state* failures (missing plate, rotated plate, reader busy, disconnected camera, unreachable device, e-stop), **not adversarial input**; nothing published tests what happens when the experiment protocol an agent reads contains injected instructions. AIRT should model MHS as a new actuation-capable tool class where the payoff of a successful prompt injection is physical rather than informational, and should build probes for: injected instructions in protocol documents, sample metadata and instrument output; agents chaining across **multiple instruments in parallel**, which Anthropic advertises as a feature; and whether the driver's declared safety limits can be read, reasoned about and approached asymptotically without tripping. AISPM should treat **MHS drivers, discovered devices, and device safety-limit metadata as new inventory entity types**, and flag agents holding MHS device grants as a distinct privilege class. It is model-agnostic and slated to be open-sourced, so this will not stay an Anthropic-only surface

findings.title: Microsoft publishes a 25-agent local-AI-agent taxonomy and discovers their MCP server configs on Windows and macOS — including four Claw-based agents Zenity has never named
findings.description: Defender for Endpoint's **local AI agent discovery** (Preview) automatically finds supported local AI agents **and their local *and remote* MCP server configurations** on onboarded Windows and macOS devices, then renders them as a **local AI agent inventory**, an **exposure map** linking agents to devices, identities and the resources those identities can reach, and **KQL advanced hunting**. Two things here are directly actionable. **First, the taxonomy is a published coverage checklist**: *CLI* — Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, **Junie CLI**, Kiro CLI, **OpenCode**, **Warp**, **Antigravity CLI**; *Desktop* — ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, **Goose**, **Hermes Agent**, **Ollama**, Perplexity, **Poe**; *Agentic IDEs* — Cursor, Devin Desktop, Kiro IDE, **Antigravity IDE**; *VS Code extensions* — Claude Code, **Cline**, Codex, **Gemini Code Assist**, GitHub Copilot, **Roo Code**; *Claw-based* — **OpenClaw, Clawpilot, QClaw, Claw/Nanobot**. The bolded names have no prior mention in this monitor's reports, and the Claw-based category in particular is an entire local-agent family Zenity has not been tracking. **Second, Microsoft's aggregation rule is a deliberate design choice Zenity should decide on consciously**: Defender "defines an agent as a combination of a user, a device, and an agent type," so Claude Code in 15 project folders is *one* entry. That is defensible for licensing and posture, but it collapses exactly the dimension that matters for blast radius — **which repositories, which working directories, and therefore which MCP configs and secrets each instance actually had in scope**. If Zenity adopts the same tuple it inherits the same blind spot; if it keeps per-workspace granularity, its counts will not reconcile with the customer's Defender console, and that discrepancy needs an answer ready. ENDPOINT should enumerate this agent list as a discovery target set, resolve each agent's MCP server configuration (remote entries especially — those are network egress grants, not local tooling), and reconcile against Defender's inventory where a customer runs both

findings.title: Defender now inspects agent-to-LLM network traffic for prompt injection, and documents its own bypass in one sentence
findings.description: **AI agent runtime protection** (Preview) blocks prompt injection at the device level by inspecting three points in the agent loop — the **user prompt**, the **pre-tool call before execution**, and the **post-tool response**. It ships two independent mechanisms, both with `Disabled`/`Audit`/`Block` modes: **`AiAgentProtection`**, which rides the agent's own vendor hook interface (**Claude Code hooks, Codex CLI hooks, GitHub Copilot CLI hooks, GitHub Copilot app hooks**), and **`AiAgentNetworkInspection`**, which inspects the **agent-to-LLM network flow in transit** for agents that expose no hook interface. The second mechanism is the finding. Microsoft is putting a TLS-terminating inspection point on the wire between local agents and model endpoints, and states the evasion condition outright: it **"doesn't support agents that use certificate pinning or HTTP/3."** That is a directly testable bypass — an agent that pins its certificate or negotiates HTTP/3 to its model endpoint is invisible to network inspection, and if it also exposes no hook interface it has **no runtime protection at all** while the tenant's console reports the feature as enabled. AIRT should build exactly that probe: enumerate which agents on a protected host pin certificates or use HTTP/3, cross it with which agents expose vendor hooks, and report the intersection as unprotected-but-believed-protected. Three secondary gaps compound it. The hook-based path covers **four agents** out of the 25+ Microsoft itself discovers, so agent-native inspection is the exception rather than the rule. There is **no native Intune policy support** — enablement is a PowerShell platform script that "Intune normally runs once," so drift after re-imaging or a failed run is silent and there is no policy object to audit. And the whole feature is off unless someone explicitly turned it on, per device, per method. AIRT should also treat the **"Suspicious AI prompt injection"** alert as a corroborating signal to ingest where present, and AISPM should treat `AiAgentProtection`/`AiAgentNetworkInspection` mode per device as a posture attribute — `Audit` is not `Block`, and Microsoft recommends organizations sit in `Audit` for weeks. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/ai-agent-runtime-protection-overview and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/configure-ai-agent-runtime-protection

findings.title: Copilot Studio ships a documented allow/block webhook for every tool invocation — and it fails open in one second, per environment, with no tenant-wide enforcement
findings.description: Copilot Studio's **external threat detection** integration (Preview) is a "bring your own protection" contract: whenever the orchestrator considers invoking a tool, it POSTs to a partner-implemented REST endpoint and honours `{"blockAction": true|false}`. The API is fully specified at `api-version=2025-05-01` with two endpoints — **`POST /validate`** for health and **`POST /analyze-tool-execution`** for the decision — and the request body is the richest agent-runtime payload Microsoft has published: **`plannerContext`** (the user message, the planner's own **`thought`** explaining why it chose this tool, **`chatHistory[]`**, and **`previousToolOutputs[]` including output values**), **`toolDefinition`** (id, type, name, description, input and output parameters), **`inputValues`** (the actual arguments about to be passed — Microsoft's own example is a `bcc` of `hacker@evil.com`), and **`conversationMetadata`** (agent id/tenant/environment/version/`isPublished`, the user's **Entra object ID**, trigger id and schema, `conversationId`, `planId`, `planStepId`, `parentAgentComponentId`). This is simultaneously an integration path Zenity can implement and a set of defects Zenity should be detecting in customer tenants. **Four of them.** *It fails open*: "The agent expects a response … within less than 1,000 ms … If your system doesn't respond in time, the agent behaves as if your response is 'allow', invoking the tool" — the default error behaviour is **Allow the agent to respond**, and flipping it to **Block the query** is an explicit opt-in, so a slow or degraded provider silently degrades to no enforcement. *It cannot be enforced centrally*: "There's no global or tenant-wide setting… no PowerShell, API, or admin center setting to enforce or propagate this configuration globally for other existing or future environments" — so protection must be re-enabled by hand on **every environment created from now on**, and a new environment is an unprotected environment by default. *It does not cover classic agents*: "External threat detection is only called on generative agents that use generative orchestration. External threat detection is skipped for classic agents." *And only one provider slot exists per environment* — configuring Defender as the provider means no other vendor is in the path. AIDR should model the `analyze-tool-execution` payload as a first-class runtime event source and, independently, AISPM should audit per environment: is a provider configured at all, is the error behaviour set to Block or left on Allow, which environments were created after the last review, and what fraction of agents in each environment are classic and therefore never evaluated. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/external-security-provider and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/external-security-webhooks-interface-developers

findings.title: Defender's real-time protection covers Agent 365 agents only through Work IQ MCP — the uncovered set is defined by which tools an agent happens to use
findings.description: Defender XDR **Security for AI** turns on **automatically, with the Enable toggle on by default**, the moment a tenant onboards to Agent 365, and it brings discovery, posture assessment via prebuilt Advanced Hunting queries, near-real-time detections and **real-time protection rules**. The rules model is a built-in **Default rule that audits all agents** plus **custom rules that block**, scoped to all or specific agents, matching on four detection types — **Secret exfiltration, Malicious content propagation, Evasion techniques, Unsafe email domain** — and writing every audited or blocked action as a behaviour to the **`BehaviorInfo`** table. Three sentences in that documentation define coverage gaps precisely enough to detect. **First**: Agent 365 real-time protection works via **Work IQ MCP**, "including invocations of customer MCP tools onboarded to Agent 365," and then — "**Agents that rely on unsupported tools or don't integrate with Work IQ MCP aren't covered.**" So an agent's protection status is a function of its *tool mix*, changes whenever a maker adds a tool, and is invisible from the agent's own configuration page. AISPM should compute, per agent, the fraction of its tools that route through Work IQ MCP and flag agents with unonboarded MCP tools as unprotected-in-practice. **Second**: the exclude-agent picker states that "**Only agents with a Microsoft Entra agent ID appear in the list**" — meaning an agent without an Entra Agent ID cannot be reasoned about by these rules at all, which makes *absence of an Entra Agent ID* a posture finding with teeth rather than a hygiene note. **Third**, and counter-intuitive: "**When a blocking rule covers an agent, near-real-time alerts aren't generated for that agent**" — turning on enforcement *removes* the alert stream for that agent, leaving only `BehaviorInfo` behaviours. Any Zenity ingestion that keys on Defender alerts will see agent coverage silently drop the day a customer moves from audit to block; the behaviours table is the durable source. Coverage also differs by platform in a way worth encoding: **Foundry agents are evaluated on user requests, agent responses, tool invocations *and* tool responses**, while **Copilot Studio agents are evaluated at tool invocation only** — so the same policy intent yields different enforcement depth depending on where the agent was built

findings.title: Agent 365 auto-ingests AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI agents with no code change, and every Entra agent identity is minted by a blueprint whose permissions are inherited by all of them
findings.description: Two structural facts from the Agent 365 developer documentation reshape how Zenity should model Microsoft agent inventory. **First, Agent 365 is now a cross-cloud registry.** For Vertex AI and Bedrock agents, "Registration … requires **no development work** — agents are **pulled automatically via the Google and Amazon APIs**. No SDK integration, no blueprint, and no code changes are required." A tenant that enables Agent 365 therefore acquires an inventory of AWS and GCP agents without those agents' owners doing anything, and Defender's discovery correspondingly spans **Copilot Studio, Foundry, AWS Bedrock and GCP Vertex AI**. AISPM must expect a customer's Microsoft-side agent inventory to contain non-Microsoft-cloud agents, must not treat an agent appearing in both Agent 365 and Zenity's AWS/GCP inventory as two agents, and should use the Agent 365 registry as a cross-check on its own cloud discovery — a Bedrock agent that Google/Amazon's APIs surfaced to Microsoft but that Zenity's AWS collector missed is a discoverable gap. **Second, the Entra agent identity blueprint is the real privilege primitive, not the agent identity.** A blueprint is "an object in Microsoft Entra ID that serves as a template for creating agent identities" and is itself a special identity type that can perform exactly one operation — provision or deprovision agent identities — using its own OAuth client ID, credentials and the **`AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager`** Graph permission. **Credentials are configured on the blueprint**, and "**OAuth permissions granted to an agent identity blueprint are granted to ALL agent identities created from that blueprint**." **Inheritable permissions** go further: "When an administrator grants permissions on the blueprint principal from an inheritable resource app, **all agent identities in that organization receive those permissions automatically**" — a single consent action that silently re-privileges every existing and future agent of that type. Conditional Access targets blueprints; disabling a blueprint kills authentication for all its identities. And blueprints can be **multitenant and published through Microsoft catalogs**, so a customer can add a *third-party* blueprint to their tenant and it can then mint agent identities there — the agent-identity equivalent of a multitenant app registration. AISPM should inventory `agentIdentityBlueprint` objects and blueprint principals as first-class entities via Microsoft Graph, map blueprint → agent identities, evaluate permissions **at the blueprint level** rather than only per agent, flag inheritable-permission grants as fan-out privilege events, flag multitenant and third-party-published blueprints present in a tenant, and treat a blueprint's `AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager` grant as an agent-minting capability. Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-agent-365/developer/ and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/agent-blueprint

findings.title: Salesforce Agentforce Operations — a GA back-office agent product reaching ERP, email and collaboration systems that this monitor has never reported
findings.description: **Agentforce Operations** has been generally available since **April 29, 2026** — the productized form of the **Regrello acquisition that closed October 1, 2025** — and returns **zero hits across every report this monitor has written**. It is not an incremental Agentforce feature; it is the extension of Agentforce agents out of CRM-adjacent front-office work and into **"the processes and systems that run the business"** — explicitly **email, ERP and collaboration tools** — for "end-to-end agentic execution across the back office," on the stated premise that "agents are designed to **complete** work rather than route it." That framing is the risk: these are write-capable agents in financial and operational systems of record, and Salesforce describes them as **"specialized back-office agents [that] autonomously perform work across disconnected systems from email to ERP."** The documented agent behaviours are specific — extracting data from complex documents, running computations, **updating credit models**, identifying compliance gaps, and performing **data verification, approvals and compliance checks** — which means an agent is executing the control that a human control-owner would otherwise perform, and the approval step itself becomes an agent action. Three inventory surfaces come with it. **Blueprints**: 30+ out-of-the-box templates (invoice auditing, onboarding, PO rescheduling) *plus* the ability to **generate blueprints from unstructured process documents** — the authoritative definition of what an agent may do can be produced by a model reading a Word document, which is both a new entity type and a new injection path into agent scope; and business users edit those processes **in plain language, without code**. **Cross-platform surfaces**: work is brought to **Slack and Microsoft Teams**, so an Agentforce agent's actions and prompts leave the Salesforce trust boundary into two other collaboration platforms Zenity monitors separately. **Flow integration**: auto-sync and the ability to **trigger actions with Salesforce Flows** was slated for beta in May 2026, connecting agent decisions to the existing Flow automation estate. AISPM should discover Agentforce Operations deployments, inventory **process blueprints** (including which were model-generated from documents, and from which documents), map each specialized agent's reach into ERP, mail and Slack/Teams connectors, and build toxic-combination rules for the pattern this product creates by design: an agent that both **performs** a business action and **approves** it, or that holds a compliance-check role over data it can itself modify. Note the discovery lesson too — this was found only because a WebSearch for late-August Salesforce news surfaced the announcement; four months of scans against the configured Salesforce URLs, all of which return 403, produced nothing

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise added five data stores and gave AirOps, Airtable and Zoho Desk write actions, including Airtable record creation
findings.description: The August 28 release-note entry brings **Campfire, Clay, CourtListener, Daloopa and MSCI** into public preview as data stores an agent can "search and read … using natural language," and — the part that matters more — grants **new actions** to three connectors that previously read: **AirOps** gains *"Update knowledge base document metadata"*, **Airtable** gains *"Create records for a table"*, and **Zoho Desk** gains *"Update event."* This is the same read-to-write drift reported on 2026-08-21 for Supabase, and it is now a pattern rather than an incident: Google keeps widening the action surface of already-connected data stores without the connector itself appearing as a new entity, so an inventory captured before the change understates what the agent can do afterward while the connector list looks unchanged. **AirOps updating knowledge-base document metadata is the sharpest of the three** — it lets an agent modify the metadata of the corpus that grounds agents, which is a self-referential integrity problem: poisoned or retitled knowledge-base entries change what future retrievals surface. Airtable record creation is straightforward agent-driven data writing into a system many organizations use as an operational database. AISPM should enumerate Gemini Enterprise data stores **with their per-connector action lists**, treat any read-to-write action addition on an existing connector as a privilege-change event requiring re-evaluation rather than a catalogue update, and specifically flag write access to knowledge-base or grounding corpora as distinct from write access to business records. The five new data stores are additional inventory entities, two of which — **Daloopa and MSCI** — are financial-data sources, matching the pattern already seen in Claude for M365's S&P Global / LSEG / Daloopa connector set. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/manage-actions and https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/msci

findings.title: Cursor Cloud Agents can now create code with no source-control connection and publish it to a live public URL
findings.description: The August 27 Cursor release removes the last two things that anchored agent-produced code to a reviewable location. **"Start from scratch"** lets a Cloud Agent begin with **no GitHub or third-party SCM connection at all** — Cursor "automatically creates an Origin repo in the background," and the user only later decides whether to name it and set visibility. So work now exists in Cursor-hosted storage *before* any repository the organization knows about is created, and if the user never clicks *Create repo*, there may be no named artifact for an inventory to find. **Port-forwarded live preview** exposes the agent's cloud environment directly to the developer's browser, and **Publish with Vercel** turns the result into a **live URL** on a connected Vercel account. Chained, that is a complete path from prompt to internet-reachable application with **no git host, no pull request, no review, and no artifact in any system the security team currently enumerates** — the agentic version of shadow IT, and a data-egress path if the agent's environment held organizational context. This extends, rather than repeats, the **Cursor Origin** git-forge finding of 2026-08-21: Origin established that Cursor hosts code; this establishes that code can now originate and terminate entirely inside Cursor and Vercel. ENDPOINT and AISPM should enumerate Origin repositories including unnamed background-created ones, treat a connected **Vercel** account on a Cursor org as a publication capability requiring inventory, and correlate published URLs back to the originating agent session and prompt. Note also, as standing context rather than a new item, that Cursor's **Google Workspace plugins** (August 3) already give agents Gmail send/read, Drive read-and-create and Calendar write — so the same agent that can publish to the internet can also read the user's mailbox. Sources: https://cursor.com/changelog/start-from-scratch and https://cursor.com/docs/origin/create-repository

platforms.name: Claude for Microsoft 365 ("Office agents") — first read; a GA product this monitor never covered
details: **Four write-capable Office agents.** Excel: cell-level-cited answers, value changes that preserve formula relationships, error-cause tracing, model generation, template population, and native operations including **sort, filter, pivot-table editing, conditional formatting and data-validation dropdowns**. PowerPoint: builds slides in the template, edits selections, generates native charts and diagrams. Word: **tracked changes and comment-thread replies** under company styles. Outlook (beta): inbox triage, draft replies and **cross-team calendar coordination via `graph.microsoft.com`**, authenticated by Entra ID Nested App Auth. Source: https://claude.com/docs/office-agents/excel

**Cross-app mode shares one conversation and one context across all four add-ins**, over a WebSocket bridge at `bridge.claudeusercontent.com`. **On by default for Pro and Max; off by default for Team and Enterprise; the toggle is per-device.** Admin control is Organization settings > Office agents > "Let Claude work across apps". It is **not supported** through Bedrock, Vertex AI, Foundry or an LLM gateway. Source: https://claude.com/docs/office-agents/work-across-apps

**Connectors and Skills.** Named connectors: **S&P Global, LSEG, Daloopa**, "plus any custom connectors your organization has enabled" — custom connectors are **remote MCP**, proxied through `mcp-proxy.anthropic.com`, and Anthropic warns they "can introduce security risks." Skills apply automatically or by `/` invocation and are downloaded over `pivot.claude.ai`. `api.anthropic.com` serves inference, file uploads, **code-execution containers** and the **MCP connector registry**. Source: https://claude.com/docs/office-agents/connectors-and-skills

**Third-party platform deployment, four paths**: LLM gateway (LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong — "matches the pattern used by Claude Code"), **Bedrock direct** (Entra ID → IAM OIDC), **Vertex AI direct** (Google OAuth), **Foundry direct** (keyless per-user Entra token or resource API key; deployment names must be default model IDs). Deployment is driven by the `claude-for-msft-365-install` **Claude Code plugin** from the `anthropics/financial-services` marketplace. Source: https://claude.com/docs/office-agents/third-party-platforms

**Anthropic's own prompt-injection warning**, verbatim: *"Only use Claude for Excel with trusted spreadsheets. Files from external sources can contain hidden instructions that manipulate the add-in into extracting data, modifying records, or performing destructive actions."* Mitigation is a per-operation user confirmation. Source: https://claude.com/docs/office-agents/excel

**Documentation contradiction to re-verify**: the Excel and work-across-apps pages still state *"Activity is not included in Enterprise audit logs or the Compliance API"*, which the 2026-08-26 release note supersedes for the Compliance API. The product docs are stale relative to the platform release notes.
