findings.title: Claude for Microsoft 365 — four write-capable agents inside Excel, Word, PowerPoint and Outlook that this monitor has never covered, GA since May 2026, with local-only chat history and no audit-log inheritance
findings.description: Anthropic's `office_agents` product surface resolves to **Claude for Microsoft 365**, a set of four Office add-ins installed from a single Microsoft AppSource listing (`WA200010725`). Excel, PowerPoint and Word reached **general availability on 2026-05-07**; Outlook is in public beta. **These are not read-only sidebars.** Claude for Excel changes cell values while preserving formula relationships, populates and generates models, traces `#REF!` and `#DIV/0` root causes, and performs **native Excel operations including sorting, filtering, pivot-table editing, conditional formatting and data-validation dropdowns**. Claude for Word **edits with tracked changes and replies inside comment threads** while preserving company styles and heading hierarchy. Claude for PowerPoint builds slides inside the corporate template and generates native charts. Claude for Outlook **triages the inbox, drafts replies and coordinates calendar availability across team members through `graph.microsoft.com`**, authenticated with Microsoft Entra ID via Nested App Auth — meaning an Anthropic-hosted add-in holds a live Graph mailbox-and-calendar token. **The four share one conversation thread and one context**, over a WebSocket bridge at `bridge.claudeusercontent.com`, and cross-app mode is **on by default on Pro and Max plans**, off by default on Team and Enterprise, with the toggle held **per device** rather than per user. **The capability surface extends well past the file.** Connectors pull external context into the workbook — Anthropic names **S&P Global, LSEG and Daloopa**, "plus any custom connectors your organization has enabled," and custom connectors are **remote MCP servers**, invoked through `mcp-proxy.anthropic.com`, about which Anthropic's own page says "Custom connectors can introduce security risks." Skills apply automatically or by `/` invocation. Per-app **persistent Instructions** apply to every conversation in that app and are set by the user in the sidebar, not by an admin. `api.anthropic.com` serves inference, file uploads, **code-execution containers** and the **MCP connector registry** for this add-in. **The reason this is an AISPM finding and not just a product note is the inventory and logging shape.** Chat history is stored **locally in the browser's IndexedDB** — "not stored on Anthropic's servers, not synced across devices" — and **survives reinstalling the add-in or switching between Claude add-ins**. The add-ins **do not inherit the organization's custom data-retention settings**. And **individual users can always self-install from the Office Store regardless of admin deployment**; the documented admin path (M365 Admin Center > Integrated apps) even fails outright when the admin's role was activated through **Entra PIM** (Microsoft tracking ID 11126536), with the documented workaround being a permanently-active admin role. So the realistic tenant state is a mix of admin-deployed and self-installed instances, each holding local conversation state, each able to reach connectors the user enabled in their own Claude settings. AISPM should inventory Claude for M365 as a first-class agent surface: enumerate the add-in per user and per host app from the M365 Integrated apps and Office add-in inventory, record whether it is admin-deployed or self-installed, read the **cross-app toggle state per device** (defaulting on for Pro/Max is the state that will surprise people), enumerate the **connector registrations** and any **custom remote-MCP connectors** as tool entities bound to the user rather than to a tenant, capture the per-app **Instructions** text as agent configuration, and treat the **Outlook Graph token** as a standing mailbox-and-calendar grant held by a third-party add-in

findings.title: Anthropic documents a working prompt-injection path into Claude for Excel — untrusted spreadsheets can drive data extraction and destructive edits, and the only control is a user confirmation click
findings.description: The Claude for Excel documentation carries a warning Anthropic wrote about its own product, and it is unusually direct. *"Only use Claude for Excel with trusted spreadsheets. Files from external sources can contain hidden instructions that manipulate the add-in into extracting data, modifying records, or performing destructive actions."* And then, on their testing rather than on theory: *"Testing has identified scenarios where Claude for Excel can be manipulated to extract sensitive information, modify critical data, or perform destructive actions if allowed to act without verification."* Anthropic names the delivery vehicles explicitly — **downloaded templates, vendor files and data imports**. **This is the highest-yield injection surface in the Office suite for three structural reasons.** **First, the carrier is a file format organisations receive constantly from outside and open without thought**, and a spreadsheet has abundant places to hide instruction text that a human reader will never see: distant cells, hidden rows and columns, defined names, comments, hidden sheets, and text in cells whose font colour matches the fill. A vendor pricing template or a downloaded model is a routine artifact, not a suspicious one. **Second, the agent reading the injected content also holds write authority over the same workbook and, in cross-app mode, over the open Word document, PowerPoint deck and Outlook thread as well** — so a payload landing in Excel can act in Outlook, which is where the exfiltration channel is. Cross-app mode being **default-on for Pro and Max** means the wide-blast-radius configuration is the one that ships enabled to the least-managed plans. **Third, the tool surface reachable from that context is not fixed**: whatever connectors the user has enabled in their Claude settings — S&P Global, LSEG, Daloopa, or an arbitrary **custom remote-MCP connector** — are available to the same reasoning loop, and MCP connectors reach outward by definition. **The documented mitigation is a per-operation user confirmation prompt**: "When Claude proposes a risky operation, you are asked to confirm before it runs." That is a click-through control, and the surrounding guidance ("review confirmations carefully, especially for files from external sources") concedes as much. There is no documented tenant-level policy, no content scanning of the workbook, and no notion of file provenance in the product. AIRT should build a purpose-made corpus against this surface and treat it as a distinct target from web and email injection: instructions hidden in non-visible cell regions, hidden sheets and defined names; payloads that exploit the agent's cited-answer behaviour by seeding the citation trail; payloads that trigger the **native operations** (a data-validation dropdown or conditional-formatting rule is an odd but real persistence and signalling mechanism inside a document that will be forwarded onward); **cross-app pivots** that read from a poisoned workbook and write to an Outlook draft or a Word document; attempts to reach an enabled connector from injected context; and payloads specifically shaped to make the confirmation prompt read as benign, since the prompt text is generated from the proposed operation. Test the Outlook direction too — an inbound email is an untrusted document reaching an agent that already holds a Graph token

findings.title: Claudeforce puts a 37-skill Salesforce plugin inside Claude and makes Claude the default model for Agentforce Coworker — an agent surface this monitor has never reported
findings.description: On **2026-08-26** Salesforce and Anthropic announced **Claudeforce**, and it runs in both directions. **Outbound from Salesforce: "Salesforce in Claude"** is a plugin carrying **37 prebuilt sales skills** — Salesforce's framing is that they are "engineered specifically for Claude's capabilities rather than generic API wrapping" — covering meeting prep, deal health review and pipeline review, and letting sellers "reason over live revenue context, **automate pipeline updates**, and **take governed action** right from Claude." It is with **select pilot customers now, with open beta expected in September 2026**, and more skills from late 2026. **This inverts the direction of every Salesforce finding this monitor has previously filed.** Until now Salesforce hosted the agent and Zenity's question was what that agent could reach. Here **the agent host is Claude** and Salesforce is the tool-and-data surface reached from outside the CRM — so the CRM's own governance sees tool invocations arriving from a session it does not host, does not log and cannot enumerate, and Zenity's Salesforce-side inventory will not contain the agent at all. Note the plugin is **not** the generic `claude.com/plugins/sales` (four commands, CRM-agnostic, MCP-connected); do not conflate them, and note there is **no public documentation page for the 37-skill plugin yet** — the announcement is the only source. **Inbound to Salesforce: Claude becomes a default model across Agentforce.** It powers the **Atlas Reasoning Engine**, is the **default for Agentforce Vibes**, is the **default model for Agentforce Coworker**, and is available in **Agent Builder**. **Agentforce Coworker is itself a coverage gap**: it appears in zero prior reports from this monitor, it is an AI teammate surfaced "in every search bar" across the Salesforce experience, and it **provisions automatically through Salesforce Foundation Flex Credits** for eligible licences — an agent that appears in a tenant without anyone deploying it, which is precisely the shape AISPM exists to catch. **Claude also becomes the backbone of Slack**, powering Slackbot, augmenting decisions through **Claude Tag** (reported 2026-07-03), and serving as a founding partner for **Slack Code**. **The deployment topology is the part to design around.** Claude is delivered **through Amazon Bedrock, inside the Salesforce Trust Boundary**, with Claude's traffic contained in Salesforce's virtual private cloud — Anthropic's partnership material calls it "the first LLM provider fully integrated within the Salesforce trust boundary." The consequence is that **no single vendor's control plane observes the whole path**: Salesforce's audit surface sees a model call it does not route externally, Anthropic's Compliance API does not cover Bedrock-routed traffic at all (its own docs exclude sessions "run through a third-party cloud platform such as Amazon Bedrock"), and AWS sees a Bedrock invocation inside someone else's VPC. AISPM should inventory Agentforce Coworker and Agentforce Vibes as agent entities with their model provenance recorded, discover which Agentforce components are on the Claude default versus an explicitly selected model, model "Salesforce in Claude" as an **external agent host holding a Salesforce grant** and inventory it from the Salesforce connected-app / OAuth side because it will not appear in the agent inventory, and flag the Bedrock-inside-Trust-Boundary path as a **logging blind spot rather than a security control** — the VPC containment is real, and so is the fact that it removes the traffic from every compliance surface Zenity currently reads

findings.title: Deploying Claude for M365 through Bedrock creates a standing Entra→AWS federation edge, and a Claude Code plugin ships per-user MCP servers through a bootstrap endpoint and Graph extension attributes
findings.description: Organizations that route AI through their own infrastructure deploy the Claude Office add-ins without individual Claude accounts, over one of **four connection paths** the IT admin picks: an **LLM gateway** (LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong — Anthropic notes it "matches the pattern used by Claude Code"), **Bedrock direct**, **Vertex AI direct**, or **Foundry direct**. End users see an identical interface either way, which means the connection path is invisible from the client and must be read from configuration. **Each path plants a durable identity artifact.** **Bedrock direct requires an IAM OIDC identity provider trusting Microsoft Entra ID tokens**, plus a role holding **`bedrock:InvokeModel` and `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`** with a trust policy scoped to the Claude add-in's application ID — a permanent, cross-cloud federation edge from the Microsoft tenant into the AWS account, created so that a spreadsheet sidebar can call a model. **Foundry direct's keyless mode** needs a customer Entra app registration with the Azure Cognitive Services **`user_impersonation`** delegated permission, admin-consented, and users holding the **Cognitive Services User** role on the resource — user-impersonation delegation granted to an add-in. **Vertex AI direct** needs a Google OAuth client with the add-in's redirect URI. **The provisioning tool is itself the finding's second half.** All of this is set up by **`claude-for-msft-365-install`**, a **Claude Code plugin** installed from the `anthropics/financial-services` marketplace and run as `/claude-for-msft-365-install:setup`. Two of its commands create ongoing configuration channels rather than one-time setup. **`:update-user-attrs` writes per-user configuration into Microsoft Graph extension attributes** — Anthropic's stated use case is "different gateway tokens or AWS roles for different teams," which means **the AWS role a given user's add-in assumes is stored as a directory attribute** and changing that attribute changes what the add-in can reach. **`:bootstrap` builds "a bootstrap endpoint for per-user MCP servers, skills, and dynamic config"** — an org-controlled URL that serves **tool surfaces and skills to individual users at runtime**, with no local manifest, no marketplace entry and no artifact on the endpoint to inventory. A third command, **`:export-data`**, makes a read-only copy of a user's chat history, skills, **connector registrations** and settings, which is worth knowing because it is the documented way to enumerate what a given user's add-in actually holds. AISPM should discover these artifacts on the identity side, where they are durable and readable: an **IAM OIDC provider whose trust is an Entra tenant** and whose role grants Bedrock invoke, an **Entra app registration with admin-consented `user_impersonation` on Cognitive Services**, a Google OAuth client bound to an add-in redirect URI, and **Graph extension attributes carrying AI routing configuration** — the last of which will not look like AI configuration to a directory scanner unless it is specifically modelled. The bootstrap endpoint should be treated as an **MCP distribution channel** and inventoried as one: it determines each user's tool surface, it is per-user, and it leaves nothing behind on the device. Note also that in third-party mode the model list comes from the platform and the admin's configuration rather than from Claude.ai model-access settings, so **model governance moves to a different control plane than the one an Anthropic-side reviewer would check**

findings.title: Anthropic's Compliance API now returns Claude Science and Claude for M365 transcripts and its Admin API moved into the CLI and seven SDKs — a new ingestion surface whose documented exclusions are the coverage map
findings.description: Two changes on **2026-08-26**. **First, the Compliance API session endpoints went GA for Cowork and Claude Code and gained two new `product_surface` families in beta**: `claude_science`, and `office_agents/excel` / `office_agents/powerpoint` / `office_agents/word` / `office_agents/outlook` (bare `office_agents` when the app is unidentified). No new key, scope, setting or client update is required — the existing **Compliance Access Key** with **`read:compliance_user_data`** covers it. The local endpoints are `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local`, `.../{session_id}` and `.../{session_id}/messages`, with IDs prefixed `clls_`. AIDR should ingest these as a first-class activity source and **branch on `product_surface`**, because an Office-agent session and a Claude Code session are different activity types with different risk shapes. Anthropic's own guidance is to build forward-compatible handlers that pass through unrecognised `product_surface` values, which is also the right ingestion posture — new surfaces will keep appearing here first, exactly as these two did. **Second, and equally useful: the Admin API is now available in the `ant` CLI (`ant beta:organization`) and in the Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby SDKs under `client.beta.organization`**, covering organization info, members, invites, workspaces and workspace members, API keys, rate limits, service accounts, **workload identity federation issuers and rules**, and **customer-managed encryption keys**. That is a programmatic control-plane surface Zenity can read for posture — and one an attacker can read too, noting that **automated workloads skip interactive login entirely and authenticate through WIF**, with the SDKs performing the token exchange from federation environment variables. **The documented exclusions are where the real value is, because they define what this ingestion will never tell you.** The session endpoints **do not return**: Claude Code authenticated with a Console API key **or run through Bedrock, Vertex AI or Foundry** — which is precisely the deployment Claudeforce and the Office add-ins' third-party mode create; **Claude Code on the web**, which runs in Anthropic's cloud but is not a remote session; **all local sessions in organizations with HIPAA readiness enabled**, where nothing is captured at all; and any session under **zero data retention**. Within a captured transcript, **thinking blocks are never included**, the **system prompt is replaced by a marker**, and **tool definitions and MCP server configuration are not part of the transcript at all** — so Zenity can see that a tool was called but not what the agent was told the tool does. Non-text tool results (web search results, code-execution output) collapse to `[N non-text item(s) not shown]`, though **the matching `tool_use` with the query or code in its `input` is still returned**, which is the single most useful retained field. Tool inputs and result text truncate at **10,000 bytes** by default (`tool_use_input_max_bytes` / `tool_result_max_bytes`, `-1` for ~1 MiB), and **a truncated `tool_use` input is no longer valid JSON** — so parse tool inputs only from untruncated blocks or raise the cap and refetch. Two ingestion traps: `created_at` **advances** as old calls age past retention, so deduplicate on `id` rather than assuming stable ordering; and the `updated_at.gte` poll bound must be set **a few minutes before** the previous run's start, because a bound set to the exact previous time "silently and permanently drops a session whose final call was still indexing at that moment." Finally, `provenance.reason = not_captured` **does not mean nothing was recorded** — Anthropic states that content withheld from the Compliance API by its data-handling policies reports the same reason. Two smaller notes worth carrying: remote sessions can be **agent-owned** (`agent_id` prefix `cagt_`, with `started_by_user` naming the initiating human), and the `user_ids[]` filter **excludes agent-owned sessions entirely** — so filtering by user hides exactly the automated runs. And **Claude Science emits separate background sessions for its own reviewer and delegation tracks**, which is a documented confirmation that Claude Science runs sub-agents

platforms.name: ChatGPT Enterprise (OpenAI) — three additions, all August 25
details: **Site tools (WebMCP) in the desktop app's built-in browser.** A page registers tools with `document.modelContext.registerTool()`, each carrying a name, description, input schema, an execute handler that calls the application's own logic, and annotations such as `readOnlyHint`. Compatible agents **discover the tools automatically** on navigation; users can inspect them via a **"Site tools" button in the address bar** and disable the feature under **Settings > Browser > Permissions**. Requires **GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra** (Luna has WebMCP disabled) and the latest desktop app. **Not available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces.** Each invocation gets a safety review and normal website-access/confirmation policies still apply for consequential actions. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/webmcp

**Browser extension expanded from Chrome to Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi**, configured under **Settings > Computer Use**, selected per chat by `@`-mention, with a per-browser **allowlist/blocklist of domains** under *Manage*. All five support tab mentions and browser control; Opera lacks side chat. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/chrome-extension

**Cloud browser website sign-in.** On eligible plans, ChatGPT Work on **web, iOS and Android** can prompt the user to sign in to a supported website **through the cloud browser**, with credentials entered in the sign-in flow rather than in chat. Cloud browser sessions are isolated from local browsers. **Excluded from Enterprise and Edu workspaces.** Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser

**Event-triggered scheduled tasks.** Tasks now fire on Gmail, Slack or GitHub events rather than a clock. Setup is **Settings > Apps** to connect the account, then describe the event and action; the user reviews **Trigger, Condition and Prompt** and completes authorization. The ChatGPT Slack app must be a member of each watched channel; the GitHub app needs repository access. Time-based schedules and event triggers **cannot coexist** on one task. Available on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, and in ChatGPT for Healthcare workspaces. Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/automations

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — one new release-note entry
details: **AWS Agent Registry: cross-account sharing with AWS RAM.** Four AWS-managed RAM permissions on the `agent-registry:Registry` resource type: **`AWSRAMDefaultPermissionAgentRegistryReadOnly`** (control-plane reads + data-plane discovery, **no** MCP invoke), **`AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForConsumer`** (discovery + **`InvokeRegistryMcp`**), **`AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForPublisher`** (Consumer + create/update/delete/`SubmitRegistryRecordForApproval`), and **`AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForAdmin`** (Publisher + **`UpdateRegistryRecordStatus`** — approve, reject, deprecate). AWS explicitly recommends **Consumer** for typical sharing. `UpdateRegistry` and `DeleteRegistry` always stay with the owner. Two service condition keys — **`agent-registry:RecordCreatorAccount`** and **`agent-registry:RecordSourceAccount`** — are resolved at authorization time from the stored record and cannot be spoofed from request input, but are **not evaluated** on `CreateRegistryRecord`, `SearchDiscoverableRegistryRecords`, `ListRegistryRecords` or `ListDiscoverableRegistryRecords`. Revocation is eventually consistent with a **~30-second** propagation delay. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/registry-cross-account-sharing.html

*(Re-verified unchanged: the data-plane Actions API is operation-for-operation identical to the 2026-08-07 capture — third consecutive verification. `SearchRegistryRecords` remains the only registry operation on that page.)*

platforms.name: Microsoft Agent Framework — first scan; two findings
details: **Agent Hooks — a first-class, fail-closed interception contract.** Implements the framework-neutral **AGENT-HOOKS-0.1** specification (`github.com/responsibleai/agent-hooks`). Eight interception points: `agent_startup`, `input`, `pre_model_call`, `post_model_call`, `pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `output`, `agent_shutdown`. Verdicts: `allow`, `warn`, `deny`, **`escalate`** (deny pending an approval resolver), and `transform` (rewrite a value under a `$target` path). Runtime guarantees: **fail closed** (invalid contexts, invalid verdicts, interceptor failures and enforcement failures all block rather than bypass), **transform write-back**, **buffered streaming** (no update reaches the caller until the complete response passes `output`), **verdict-gated persistence**, and **complete bundle installation** (agent + chat + function parts install as one unit). Configuration includes `mode` (`enforce` vs **`evaluate_only`**), `composition` (default sequential `first_deny`), `identity_provider` (default `jcs-sha256`), a 5-second per-interceptor `timeout`, and a `record_sink` that receives **payload-free** `InterceptionRecord`s. **Python only and experimental**; not implemented in .NET or Go. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/agents/agent-hooks

**FIDES — deterministic information-flow control against prompt injection and exfiltration.** Every `Content` item carries a `security_label` with **integrity** (`trusted` / `untrusted`) and **confidentiality** (`public` / `private` / `user_identity`); `combine_labels` picks the most restrictive of each axis. Four parts: `ContentLabel`, `LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware`, `PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware`, and `quarantined_llm` + `ContentVariableStore`. Sinks annotate `accepts_untrusted: False` and `max_allowed_confidentiality`; sources annotate per-item labels or a tool-level `source_integrity`. `SecureAgentConfig` wires it up as a **context provider**, with `auto_hide_untrusted` (default **True** — untrusted results are replaced in the main context by a `var_<id>` reference), secure-by-default `default_integrity=UNTRUSTED`, `allow_untrusted_tools`, `block_on_violation`, `approval_on_violation`, `enable_audit_log` and `enable_policy_enforcement`. `quarantined_llm` processes untrusted variables against a separate chat client **with no tools attached**, and labels its own output untrusted. Experimental, **Python only**, documented since **ms.date 2026-06-23** (`updated_at` 2026-08-25). Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/agents/security

*(Held: `python-1.15.0` optional **A2UI** support for agent-generated interfaces — A2UI itself was reported 2026-08-21; A2A preview consent URLs; Foundry Hosted Agents steering/retry/recovery; `dotnet-1.19.0` session-persisted chat routing, Azure Blob Storage session persistence, hosted agent state in Foundry, and the breaking migration of MCP long-running task support to the **2026-07-28 Tasks extension**; `dotnet-1.18.0` A2A task store isolation and a Cosmos chat-history retrieval API.)*

findings.title: OpenAI site tools (WebMCP) — any website can hand tools to a visiting ChatGPT or Codex agent, with no install, no config file, and tool definitions that OpenAI documents as untrusted
findings.description: On **August 25, 2026** OpenAI shipped **site tools**, its implementation of the proposed **WebMCP** standard, in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser and in ChatGPT Sites. A page registers a tool by calling **`document.modelContext.registerTool()`** in ordinary JavaScript, supplying a name, a description, an input schema, an **execute handler that calls the application's existing logic**, and annotations such as `readOnlyHint`. A compatible agent — **ChatGPT Work or Codex** — **discovers the available tools automatically when the page loads** and invokes the relevant ones while completing the user's task. **Every assumption behind existing tool inventory breaks here.** There is no installation event, so nothing is ever written to disk or to a settings file; there is no marketplace or registry, so there is no catalogue to enumerate; there is no server, so there is no endpoint to inspect out-of-band; and the tool set **exists only for the lifetime of the page**, which means an agent's capability set is now a function of navigation history rather than configuration. This is a different problem from the Agent Plugins/`mcp.json` gap reported on 08-24 — that was an artifact in the wrong file, this is **no artifact at all**. OpenAI's own documentation supplies the threat model in its own words: "**Website-provided tool definitions and results are untrusted content**", "**tool names alone don't prove function or scope**", "website instructions don't grant permission for unrelated actions", and, on its mitigations, "**these checks reduce risk; they don't make a website or its output trustworthy**." Three specifics make this actionable. **First, tools run inside the site's existing authenticated session** — the execute handler is the site's own code calling its own logic with the logged-in user's permissions, so a site tool's blast radius is exactly what the user can do on that site, reached without the user clicking anything. **Second, the mitigations are per-invocation and local**: each invocation gets a safety review, the browser ties invocations to the originating page, normal website-access and confirmation policies still apply for consequential actions (sending messages, purchases, deleting data, changing permissions), and users can inspect the tool list via a **"Site tools" button in the address bar** or disable the feature under **Settings > Browser > Permissions** — all of which are user-facing controls with no tenant-level policy surface documented. **Third, and most important for coverage: it is withheld from Enterprise and Edu workspaces**, and it requires **GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra** (Luna has it disabled). So the population that has it is Plus/Pro/Business on a personal or unmanaged-tier account — precisely the population an enterprise sees least. AIRT should treat a WebMCP-enabled page as a first-class injection and tool-abuse vector, and test the specific shape this creates: a tool whose *description* is adversarial (the model chooses tools by description, and the description is attacker-authored), a tool whose *name* implies a benign scope while its handler does something else (OpenAI names this failure explicitly), a `readOnlyHint` annotation that is simply false, and tool *results* used to steer subsequent turns. ENDPOINT must stop treating tool availability as static endpoint state: capability now arrives per-navigation, so the signal to collect is browsing-plus-invocation telemetry from the desktop app, not a file inventory. AISPM should model "site tool" as an ephemeral tool entity bound to an origin rather than to an agent or an install, and treat the **origin** as the provenance record it will never get from a manifest

findings.title: ChatGPT scheduled tasks can now be triggered by inbound Gmail, Slack and GitHub events — an outsider who can email the user can cause an authenticated agent to run
findings.description: Also on **August 25, 2026**, OpenAI made scheduled tasks event-driven. A task can now fire on **a new Gmail message** (optionally filtered by sender or subject), **a new message in a watched Slack channel**, or **pull-request activity in an authorized github.com repository** — including reviews, comments, commit updates and merges. The user connects the account under **Settings > Apps**, describes the event and the action in Work, then reviews a **Trigger, Condition and Prompt** triple and completes authorization. The **ChatGPT Slack app must be a member of every watched channel** and the **GitHub app needs repository access**, so the trigger carries its own standing integration grant. Time-based schedules and event triggers **cannot coexist** on a single task, and **clustered events may be combined into a single run**. Available on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu, plus ChatGPT for Healthcare workspaces. **The security consequence is a change in who initiates agent activity.** Until now an agent run in ChatGPT was traceable to a human action — a prompt, or a schedule that a human set. An event trigger inverts this: **the initiating party is whoever authored the triggering content**, and for the three named sources that party is frequently external. Anyone who can send the user an email, post in a Slack channel the ChatGPT app has joined, or comment on a pull request in an authorized repo can now cause an authenticated agent run to happen, at a time of their choosing, on text they wrote. That is the classic indirect-prompt-injection precondition with the delivery problem solved for the attacker: they no longer need the user to paste anything or open anything. **The filters are the attack surface, not the control** — "filter by sender or subject" is attacker-observable and attacker-satisfiable, and a sender filter is only as strong as the absence of spoofing and forwarding. Two second-order properties matter for detection. **Event clustering** means one agent run may correspond to several triggering messages, so the mapping from external content to agent action is many-to-one and cannot be reconstructed from the run alone. And because triggers are configured per task with their own connected app, **the standing grant outlives the user's attention**: a task configured once keeps consuming external content indefinitely with no session for a human to be present in. AIDR should treat event-triggered task runs as a distinct activity type from user-initiated and schedule-initiated runs, capture the triggering source (Gmail sender/subject, Slack channel and author, GitHub repo/PR/actor) as first-class attribution, and alert on the shape that matters: an externally-triggered run that subsequently touches internal data or invokes a write-capable connector. AISPM should inventory event-triggered tasks as standing automations with an external trigger surface, record which apps each is bound to and which channels/repos are watched, and flag tasks whose trigger is broad (any new Gmail message, a high-traffic public channel, a repo with external contributors)

findings.title: AWS Agent Registry can now be shared across accounts via RAM, and three of the four managed permissions grant live MCP invocation — with automatic acceptance inside an Organization
findings.description: AWS added **cross-account sharing to the AWS Agent Registry** through **AWS Resource Access Manager**. The registry — the "private, governed catalog of agents, tools, skills, MCP servers, and custom resources" reported on 2026-08-07 — is now a shareable RAM resource type (`agent-registry:Registry`), and the owner selects one of four AWS managed permissions that RAM enforces through a resource-based policy it manages. **The permission tiers are the finding.** `AWSRAMDefaultPermissionAgentRegistryReadOnly` (the default when no permission is specified) grants control-plane reads plus data-plane discovery but **explicitly not** MCP invocation. `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForConsumer` grants discovery **plus `agent-registry:InvokeRegistryMcp`** — and AWS's own tip recommends it as the default choice: "We recommend the **Consumer** permission for typical sharing scenarios." `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForPublisher` adds `CreateRegistryRecord`, `UpdateRegistryRecord`, `DeleteRegistryRecord` and `SubmitRegistryRecordForApproval`. `AWSRAMPermissionAgentRegistryForAdmin` adds **`UpdateRegistryRecordStatus`** — approve, reject or deprecate records — so **curation authority over a registry can be delegated to a different AWS account** while `UpdateRegistry`/`DeleteRegistry` stay with the owner. Read together: the recommended sharing posture is not "let another account look at the catalogue", it is "**let another account's agents invoke tools through my registry's MCP endpoint**", and the most permissive tier lets a foreign account decide which records are approved for everyone. **The consent model is the second half.** For accounts outside the owner's Organization, RAM sends an invitation the consumer must accept. **For accounts inside the same Organization with RAM org-sharing enabled, acceptance is automatic — no invitation, no consumer-side action, no event for the consumer to notice.** So in the common enterprise case, a registry share simply appears, and any Zenity model that expects a two-sided handshake will miss it entirely. Revocation is likewise **eventually consistent, with up to ~30 seconds of continued access after `disassociate-resource-share`**. **Third, the fine-grained controls have a documented enumeration hole.** The two service condition keys — **`agent-registry:RecordCreatorAccount`** and **`agent-registry:RecordSourceAccount`** — are resolved at authorization time from the stored record and cannot be set from request input (good), but AWS states they are **not evaluated** on `CreateRegistryRecord`, nor on **`SearchDiscoverableRegistryRecords`, `ListRegistryRecords` or `ListDiscoverableRegistryRecords`**, which "return summaries for all matching records regardless of condition-key restrictions." AWS's own remediation is to withhold search and list from the share — which almost nobody will do, because discovery is the point. So a consumer scoped by condition key to its own records can still **enumerate the full catalogue of another account's agents, tools and MCP servers**. AISPM should treat a shared registry as a cross-account trust edge, not an attribute: discover RAM resource shares over `agent-registry:Registry`, resolve which managed (or customer-managed) permission each carries, and materially distinguish shares that include `InvokeRegistryMcp` from those that don't. Flag `ForAdmin` shares as delegated curation authority, flag org-internal shares as having no acceptance event, flag any customer-managed permission that grants list/search alongside condition keys as an enumeration exposure, and correlate registry records against the consumer accounts that can reach them so a "private, governed catalog" is not scored as single-account when it is not

findings.title: Microsoft Agent Hooks — a framework-neutral, fail-closed agent interception contract with eight named control points and three documented bypasses
findings.description: Microsoft Agent Framework has shipped **Agent Hooks**, described by Microsoft as "a first-class Agent Framework capability for applying governance and runtime controls at well-defined points in an agent's execution," and it implements **AGENT-HOOKS-0.1**, a **framework-neutral contract** published at `github.com/responsibleai/agent-hooks` so that "policy engines, approval gateways, budget guards, content filters, and egress controls can target one common control surface." It reached first-class experimental status in **.NET 1.19.0 on August 22** and is experimental in the Python SDK; the doc pages were refreshed **2026-08-25**. **Why this is a coverage item and not just a competitor feature:** Agent Hooks is where an enterprise's agent controls will increasingly live, so Zenity needs to inventory it, read its verdicts, and know exactly where its guarantees stop. **The control surface is eight named interception points** — `agent_startup`, `input`, `pre_model_call`, `post_model_call`, `pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `output`, `agent_shutdown` — each with a defined transform target (messages to the model, tool arguments, tool results, final response content). **The verdict vocabulary is five-valued**: `allow`, `warn`, `deny`, **`escalate`** (a liftable deny resolved through an approval channel), and `transform` (rewrite a value at a `$target` path). Microsoft states the runtime guarantees explicitly: **fail closed** — "invalid contexts, invalid verdicts, interceptor failures, and enforcement failures don't silently bypass controls"; **transform write-back**, where a transform that can't be applied fails the run; **buffered streaming**, where no update reaches the caller until the full response has passed `post_model_call` and `output`; **verdict-gated persistence**; and **complete bundle installation**, so "an incomplete enforcement boundary can't be configured accidentally." **The three bypasses Microsoft documents are the highest-value part of this finding, because each is a place where a customer will believe they are protected and not be.** (1) **Provider-executed hosted tools do not pass through the function-invocation seam at all** — their calls and outputs surface at `post_model_call`, but `pre_tool_call` and `post_tool_call` "can't block the provider's server-side execution." An agent whose tools are hosted by the model provider therefore has *no* enforceable tool gate, only after-the-fact visibility. (2) **Middleware registered before the bundle is outside the boundary** — "treat outer position as outer trust" — so ordering, not presence, determines coverage, and a misordered stack silently reduces the enforcement surface. (3) **The contract is "cooperative rather than a process isolation boundary"**: interceptors run in the host process, receive the full content, and are not sandboxed — "only register interceptors you trust", and "code paths that bypass the guarded agent pipeline aren't covered." A fourth, subtler gap sits in persistence: with `require_per_service_call_history_persistence=True`, each model exchange is persisted once its `post_model_call` verdict permits it, and **"a later `output` deny doesn't roll back that already permitted history"** — so an output-only egress policy leaves model content durable. **And the mode flag is a posture attribute in its own right**: `evaluate_only` runs every interceptor and records every verdict while **allowing every action**, with Microsoft warning "don't describe an `evaluate_only` deployment as enforced governance." An agent with hooks installed in `evaluate_only` looks governed and is not — exactly the kind of false-assurance state AISPM exists to surface. Note also the availability asymmetry: **Python only**; .NET and Go agents are directed to plain middleware, tool approval and Agent Safety instead, so within one customer's fleet the same nominal control exists on some agents and not others. AISPM should discover which Agent Framework agents have an Agent Hooks bundle installed, record the **mode** (`enforce` vs `evaluate_only`), the **composition** profile (default is sequential `first_deny`), whether a `resolver` is configured (without one, every `escalate` is simply a deny), the interceptor set and its **order relative to other middleware**, and whether the agent uses provider-hosted tools — because that last fact converts a nominally complete boundary into an incomplete one. The **`record_sink` `InterceptionRecord` stream** is a first-class ingestion target for AIDR: it carries decision, reason, interceptor summary, mode, identity and sequence, deliberately **without the intercepted payload**, which makes it high-signal and low-sensitivity — but also means Zenity cannot reconstruct *what* was blocked from the record alone

findings.title: Microsoft FIDES — deterministic information-flow control with trust and confidentiality labels on agent content, shipping in Agent Framework and never reported by this monitor
findings.description: **FIDES** (Flow Integrity Deterministic Enforcement System) is information-flow control as first-class middleware in Microsoft Agent Framework, based on the [FIDES paper by Costa et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23643), shipping in `agent-framework-core` behind `agent_framework.security` as an experimental feature. It has been documented since **ms.date 2026-06-23** — this is a **two-month coverage gap**, surfaced only because the page was refreshed **2026-08-25**. Microsoft's framing is a direct attack on the heuristics Zenity's customers currently rely on: defensive system prompts and hand-rolled allow-lists "are heuristic… they don't make the next attack impossible," sanitization "is lossy," and "pre/post-hoc monitoring detects damage; it doesn't prevent it." **The mechanism is a two-axis label on every piece of content.** **Integrity** is `trusted` (developer-controlled: system prompt, internal database, signed config) or `untrusted` ("anything the model could have been tricked into ingesting — issue bodies, emails, scraped pages, third-party API responses"). **Confidentiality** is `public`, `private`, or `user_identity` (PII, credentials, per-user secrets). Labels combine **most-restrictive-wins** (`untrusted` beats `trusted`; `user_identity` > `private` > `public`) and propagate automatically through tool calls via `LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware`. **Sinks declare what context they will run in**, and these two annotations are the enforcement primitive worth internalizing: **`accepts_untrusted: False`** refuses a tool outright when anything untrusted is in scope (intended for "file writes, destructive operations, anything that mutates production state"), and **`max_allowed_confidentiality`** caps what a sink may leak (`public` for anything that publishes externally). `PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware` checks each invocation **before the tool runs**. There is also a strong-isolation mode: with **`auto_hide_untrusted=True` (the default)**, untrusted tool results never reach the main model at all — they are stashed in a `ContentVariableStore` and replaced in context by a **`var_<id>` reference**, and the agent must call **`quarantined_llm`** to process them, which dispatches an isolated completion against a separate chat client **with no tools attached** and labels its own output untrusted. **Three things make this directly actionable for Zenity.** **First, it is a ready-made vocabulary for findings Zenity already produces.** "Untrusted content reached a privileged sink" and "private content reached a public sink" are now *named, vendor-documented* conditions with a deterministic definition, on a Microsoft-supported runtime. Zenity's own toxic-combination model should adopt this framing — an agent whose reachable tool set contains a sink with no `accepts_untrusted` declaration, or whose `max_allowed_confidentiality` cap is looser than its data sources, is a computable posture defect rather than a judgement call. **Second, its configuration surface is a posture surface with real false-assurance states.** `enable_policy_enforcement=False` is the documented **dry-run mode**: labels still propagate, the audit log still fills, and **no sink is ever blocked** — an agent in this state produces governance telemetry while enforcing nothing. `approval_on_violation=True` converts blocks into human approval prompts, which means the control's effectiveness collapses to user click-through behaviour. `allow_untrusted_tools` is an explicit per-tool exemption list. And **`default_integrity` can be flipped from the secure-by-default `UNTRUSTED` to `TRUSTED`**, which silently relabels every unannotated tool's output as safe. Each of these is a discoverable configuration Zenity should read and score. **Third, its documented limitations are a coverage map.** Labels are **opt-in per data source** — "a tool you forget to label" falls back to defaults; propagation is conservative, so "once an untrusted issue body enters the context, the rest of the run is untrusted unless you explicitly drop it" (and the *drop* is where a bypass would live); approvals are coarse and don't expose the label algebra to the approving user; `quarantined_llm` is **single-turn and tools-free**, so multi-turn quarantined processing is unsupported. It is also **Python only** — .NET and Go agents get Agent Safety guidance and tool approval instead. AIRT should build test cases directly against this model: content that acquires a `trusted` label it shouldn't (a tool that returns third-party data without `source_integrity`), a sink reachable in untrusted context because it was never annotated, an exfiltration path through a sink whose cap is `user_identity`, label-laundering through a transformation tool, and injection delivered through `quarantined_llm` output — which is labeled untrusted but is still text the main model reasons over. AISPM should inventory FIDES adoption per agent, extract the label declarations on sources and sinks, and flag the four false-assurance configurations above

findings.title: ChatGPT's browser extension now covers Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi, and the cloud browser can collect website credentials on web and mobile
findings.description: Two extensions of the browser-control surface reported on 2026-08-07, both **August 25**. **The extension footprint quadrupled**: ChatGPT's browser extension now works in **Microsoft Edge, Brave, Opera and Vivaldi** alongside Chrome, installed through **Settings > Computer Use** in the desktop app (with a "More browsers" expansion for browsers not listed), selected per chat by `@`-mention against the specific browser profile where the extension was installed. All five support tab mentions and browser control; Opera lacks side chat. Domain policy is per-browser and user-managed: **Manage** next to a browser exposes an **allowlist** of domains ChatGPT may use without asking again and a **blocklist** of domains it shouldn't touch. The coverage consequence is concrete: any ENDPOINT collector that detects ChatGPT browser control by looking for the Chrome extension ID, or that enumerates one browser's extension inventory, now under-reports on four additional browsers — and it under-reports on the **profile** dimension too, since the grant is per-browser-profile and the same machine can hold several. The **per-browser allowlist/blocklist is also new inventory**: it is the closest thing to a domain policy on this surface, it is set by the user rather than an admin, and its contents (particularly a broad allowlist) are a posture attribute worth reading. **The cloud browser can now take website credentials.** On eligible plans, ChatGPT Work on **web, iOS and Android** can prompt the user to "sign in to a supported website through the cloud browser," with **login details entered inside the sign-in flow rather than in chat** — an explicit design choice to keep credentials out of the conversation, which also means the authentication event does not appear in the transcript. Cloud browser sessions are documented as **isolated from local browsers**, so the resulting authenticated session lives entirely in OpenAI-hosted infrastructure: a durable, agent-usable session against a third-party site that exists on no endpoint Zenity can inspect and in no local browser profile. Both features are **excluded from Enterprise and Education workspaces**, which is the same asymmetry as the site-tools finding — the capability lands on the least-managed tiers. ENDPOINT should enumerate the ChatGPT extension across all five browsers and all profiles, read the per-browser allowlist/blocklist as policy state, and treat cloud-browser website sign-in as an off-endpoint session grant that must be inventoried from the ChatGPT side because it is invisible locally. AIDR should treat a cloud-browser authentication event as a distinct activity type from a local browser-control session. Sources: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/chrome-extension and https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise added eight data stores and gave existing connectors write actions, including Supabase `execute SQL`, `apply migration` and `deploy edge function`
findings.description: Google's Gemini Enterprise connector surface grew twice in five days. **August 21 added seven data stores in Public Preview** — **Atlan** (data catalog/governance metadata), **Bitly**, **FactSet AI-Ready Data** (licensed financial data), **FullStory** (session replay and product analytics, i.e. recorded user behaviour), **Globalping**, **Pendo** and **Stripe** (payments) — each searchable and readable with natural language. **August 24 added the D&B Commercial Graph data store in Preview**, for searching and importing company data. Each is a new grounding source and therefore a new inventory entity, and the mix matters: FullStory and Stripe reach behavioural and payment data respectively, Atlan reaches the metadata that describes where everything else lives, and FactSet and D&B carry licensing obligations that make onward flow a compliance question, not just a security one. **But the sharper part of this release is the action expansion, because the actions are not reads.** Existing connectors gained: **Supabase — apply migration, deploy edge function, execute SQL, pause project, restore project**; **Descript — import media, prompt project agent, publish project**; **Gamma — generate Gamma**. The Supabase set alone is a database and serverless-platform control plane: `execute SQL` is arbitrary query execution, `apply migration` is schema change, `deploy edge function` is **code deployment**, and `pause project` / `restore project` are availability operations. A Gemini Enterprise agent holding these actions is not grounding on Supabase, it is **operating** Supabase — and `deploy edge function` in particular means an agent steered by untrusted grounding content can put attacker-influenced code into a running environment. `Descript — publish project` is likewise an external-publication sink. This is the pattern reported for custom MCP data stores on 2026-08-09 arriving through the first-party connector catalogue instead: the connector inventory can no longer be read as a list of data sources, because some entries are action grants with side effects. AISPM should inventory each new data store as a grounding source with its own sensitivity and licensing attributes, and — more importantly — should classify connector **actions** by effect rather than treating "connector attached" as one fact: separate read actions from write/deploy/destructive actions, flag any agent holding `execute SQL`, `apply migration` or `deploy edge function`, and treat the combination of an untrusted-content grounding source plus a write-capable connector action on the same agent as a toxic combination. Note the documented deployment constraint that helps here: Google recommends associating only one data store with actions belonging to a single connector type per app, and the Supabase data store is supported only in the `global`, `us` and `eu` locations. Sources: https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/supabase and https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise data-connector telemetry now identifies which connector tool an agent invoked and how long it took — an ingestion opportunity with a six-week retention cliff
findings.description: On **August 24** Google extended Cloud Monitoring telemetry for Gemini Enterprise data connectors in two ways. The existing count metric **`discoveryengine.googleapis.com/dataconnector/request_count`** gained three dimensions on top of its existing `status`: **`tool_id`** — "the identifier of the connector tool invoked" — **`engine_id`**, the Gemini Enterprise app identifier, and **`response_code`**, the gRPC response status. And a **new metric, `discoveryengine.googleapis.com/dataconnector/request_latencies` (Beta)**, reports "the distribution of tool invocation latency" in milliseconds with dimensions `status`, `response_code`, `tool_id` and `engine_id`. **The `tool_id` dimension is the part that changes what Zenity can see.** Until now this metric answered "how many connector requests, and did they succeed"; it now answers "**which connector tool, in which app, with what result**" — which is per-tool invocation attribution on a platform where the previous best signal was the `execute_tool` / `invoke_connector` trace spans reported on 2026-08-09. Paired with the previous finding, this is the detection layer for exactly the risk that finding describes: a Supabase `execute SQL` or `deploy edge function` invocation is now distinguishable by `tool_id` from a benign read, and attributable to a specific `engine_id`. AIDR should ingest both metrics, key on `tool_id` to build per-tool invocation baselines per app, and use `response_code` and the latency distribution as anomaly inputs — an unusual `tool_id` appearing under an `engine_id` that has never invoked it, a spike in denied `response_code`s (reconnaissance), or a latency profile shift on a write action are all detectable here and nowhere else on this platform. **Two caveats must ship with the ingestion.** These are **metrics, not logs** — they carry dimensions, counts and distributions, not arguments, results or the identity of the invoking user, so they establish *that* a named tool was invoked under an app, never *what* it did or *for whom*; correlating to a principal still requires the audit-log and trace surfaces. And retention is short: Gemini Enterprise metrics publish under the **`discoveryengine.googleapis.com/`** prefix, which falls in Google's "all other Google Cloud metrics" tier and is **retained six weeks by default** — so any investigation reaching back further than ~42 days finds nothing unless Zenity or the customer has already exported it. `request_latencies` is **Beta**, so its dimension set may still change
